title: Book Three (1805) — Chapter 7
paragraphs: On the twelfth of November, Kutuzov's army was camped outside Olmutz, preparing for a review the next day by both Emperors — Russian and Austrian. The Guards, having just arrived from Russia, spent the night ten miles away and were to march straight to the review field at Olmutz by ten the next morning.

That day, Nicholas Rostov received a letter from Boris saying that the Ismaylov regiment was camped ten miles from Olmutz for the night, and that Boris wanted to see him because he had a letter and money for him. Rostov badly needed money just then. Now that the troops were stationed near Olmutz after their active campaigning, the camp was swarming with well-stocked merchants and Austrian Jews selling all kinds of tempting goods. The Pavlograds threw one celebration after another to mark the awards they'd earned during the campaign, and made regular trips to Olmutz to visit a certain Caroline the Hungarian, who had recently opened a restaurant there with girls as waitresses. Rostov, who had just celebrated his promotion to cornet and bought Denisov's horse Bedouin, was in debt to everyone — his comrades and the merchants alike. When he got Boris's letter, he rode to Olmutz with a fellow officer, had dinner, drank a bottle of wine, and then set off alone to the Guards' camp to find his childhood friend. He hadn't had time to get a proper uniform yet. He wore a shabby cadet jacket with a soldier's cross pinned to it, equally worn cadet riding breeches with leather patches, and an officer's saber with a sword knot. The Don horse he rode was one he'd bought from a Cossack during the campaign, and he wore a crumpled hussar cap pushed jauntily to one side. As he rode toward the camp, he imagined the impression he would make on Boris and his Guards comrades — that of a battle-hardened hussar who had actually been under fire.

The Guards had marched the whole way as if on a pleasure trip, showing off their cleanliness and discipline. They'd traveled in easy stages, their packs carried on carts, and the Austrian authorities had provided excellent dinners for the officers at every stop. The regiments had entered and left each town with bands playing, and by the Grand Duke's orders, the men had marched in perfect step the entire way — a point of pride for the Guards — with officers on foot at their proper posts. Boris had been quartered and had marched all the way with Berg, who now commanded a company. Berg had earned his captaincy during the campaign and had won his superiors' trust through his punctuality and precision. He'd also managed his finances very satisfactorily. During the campaign, Boris had made the acquaintance of several useful people and, armed with a letter of introduction from Pierre, had gotten to know Prince Andrew Bolkonsky, through whom he hoped to land a position on the commander-in-chief's staff. Berg and Boris, rested after yesterday's march, were sitting clean and neatly dressed at a round table in their tidy quarters, playing chess. Berg held a lit pipe between his knees. Boris, with his characteristic precision, was building a little pyramid of chess pieces with his slender white fingers while waiting for Berg's move, his mind clearly focused entirely on the game — as was always the case with whatever he happened to be doing.
"Well, how are you going to get out of that?" he said.
"I'll figure something out," Berg replied, touching a pawn and then pulling his hand back.
At that moment the door opened.

"Here he is at last!" Rostov shouted. "And Berg too! Oh, you little kids, go to sleep!" he exclaimed, mangling the French phrase the way his Russian nanny used to, which he and Boris had always found hilarious.
"My goodness, how you've changed!"

Boris stood up to greet Rostov, but carefully steadied some chess pieces that were about to topple over. He moved to embrace his friend, but Nicholas dodged him. With that instinct of youth — the fear of well-worn paths, the desire to express itself differently from older people who are often insincere — Nicholas wanted to do something distinctive when greeting his friend. He wanted to poke him, shove him, anything but kiss him, which was what everyone did. But Boris embraced him anyway, calmly and warmly, and kissed him three times.

They hadn't seen each other for nearly half a year, and at the age when young men are taking their first steps in life, each saw enormous changes in the other — a whole new reflection of the world they'd each entered. Both had changed drastically since their last meeting, and both were eager to show off the transformations.

"Oh, you pampered dandies! Clean and polished like you're going to a ball — not like us poor infantry sinners," Rostov cried with military swagger, his voice now carrying new baritone notes that were unfamiliar to Boris, as he pointed at his own mud-splattered breeches. The German landlady, hearing Rostov's booming voice, stuck her head through the door.
"Hey — is she pretty?" he asked with a wink.

"Why are you yelling like that? You'll scare them!" Boris said. "I wasn't expecting you today. I only sent the note yesterday through Bolkonsky — one of Kutuzov's adjutants, a friend of mine. I didn't think he'd deliver it so fast... So, how are you? Have you been under fire yet?" Boris asked.
Instead of answering, Rostov shook the soldier's Cross of St. George pinned to his jacket, indicated his bandaged arm, and looked at Berg with a smile.
"See for yourself," he said.

"Really? Well, well!" said Boris, smiling. "We've had quite a fine march ourselves, you know. His Imperial Highness rode with our regiment the entire time, so we had every comfort and advantage. The receptions we got in Poland! The dinners and balls! You wouldn't believe it. And the Tsarevich was very gracious to all the officers."
And so the two friends traded stories — one about his hussar adventures and life on the front lines, the other about the pleasures and perks of serving under members of the Imperial family.
"Oh, you Guards!" said Rostov. "Hey, send for some wine."
Boris made a face.
"If you really want it," he said.
He went to his bed, pulled a purse from under the spotless pillow, and sent for wine.
"Yes, and I have some money and a letter to give you," he added.

Rostov took the letter and, tossing the money onto the sofa, propped both arms on the table and began to read. After a few lines, he glanced angrily at Berg, then, catching his eye, hid his face behind the letter.
"Well, they've sent you a nice sum," said Berg, eyeing the heavy purse sinking into the sofa cushions. "As for us, Count, we get along on our pay. Speaking for myself..."

"Listen, Berg, my dear fellow," Rostov said, "when you get a letter from home and run into someone you've known all your life and want to pour your heart out to — and I happen to be there — I'll leave immediately so I'm not in the way. Please go somewhere, anywhere... go to hell!" he burst out, then immediately grabbed Berg by the shoulder and, looking kindly into his face to soften the harshness, added: "Don't take offense, old friend. I'm speaking from the heart, as one old acquaintance to another."
"Oh, not at all, Count! I completely understand," said Berg, getting up and speaking in his muffled, throaty voice.
"Go visit our hosts — they invited you," Boris added.

Berg put on his cleanest coat — without a single spot or speck of dust — stood before a mirror and brushed his temple hair upward in the style made fashionable by Emperor Alexander. Having satisfied himself from Rostov's glance that his coat had been noticed, he left the room with a pleased smile.
"Oh God, what a beast I am!" Rostov muttered as he read the letter.
"Why?"

"What a horrible person I am — not writing to them and giving them such a scare! What a horrible person!" he repeated, suddenly flushing. "Well, has Gabriel gone for the wine? Good — let's have some!"

Enclosed with his parents' letter was a letter of recommendation to Bagration, which the old countess had obtained through a connection at Anna Mikhaylovna's suggestion and sent along for Nicholas to deliver and make use of.
"What nonsense! As if I need this!" said Rostov, tossing the letter under the table.
"Why did you throw that away?" Boris asked.
"It's some letter of recommendation... what the hell do I need it for!"
"What do you mean, 'what the hell'?" said Boris, picking it up and reading the address. "This letter could be extremely useful to you."
"I don't need anything, and I refuse to be anyone's errand boy."
"Why not?" Boris asked.
"It's a lackey's job!"
"You're still the same dreamer, I see," Boris remarked, shaking his head.
"And you're still the same diplomat! But that's beside the point... Come on, how are things with you?" Rostov asked.
"Well, as you can see, everything's fine so far. But I'll admit I'd really like to become an adjutant rather than stay at the front."
"Why?"
"Because once a man enters military service, he should try to make the most successful career of it that he can."
"Ah, is that so?" Rostov said, clearly thinking about something else.
He stared intently and searchingly into his friend's eyes, as though trying in vain to find the answer to some question.
Old Gabriel brought in the wine.
"Should we send for Berg?" Boris asked. "He'll drink with you. I can't."
"Sure, send for him... So how do you get along with that German?" Rostov asked with a dismissive smile.
"He's a very, very nice, honest, and pleasant fellow," Boris replied.

Again Rostov studied Boris's eyes intently, then sighed. Berg came back, and the three officers' conversation grew lively over the bottle of wine. The Guardsmen told Rostov about their march and how warmly they'd been received in Russia, Poland, and abroad. They talked about the Grand Duke — his sayings and habits — and shared stories of his kindness and his terrible temper. Berg, as usual, stayed quiet whenever the subject didn't concern him, but when it came to stories about the Grand Duke's outbursts, he eagerly described how, during an inspection in Galicia, he had handled the Grand Duke's fury. With a self-satisfied smile, Berg recounted how the Grand Duke had ridden up to him in a rage, shouting "Arnauts!" — the Tsarevich's favorite word when he was furious — and demanded to see the company commander.

"Would you believe it, Count — I wasn't the least bit nervous, because I knew I was in the right. Without meaning to boast, I can say that I know the Army Regulations by heart, as well as I know the Lord's Prayer. So there's never any sloppiness in my company, and my conscience was clear. I stepped forward..." Berg stood up to demonstrate how he'd presented himself, hand at his cap, and it would have been hard to find a face expressing greater self-respect and self-satisfaction. "Well, he stormed at me — stormed and stormed and stormed! It wasn't about life so much as death, as the saying goes. 'Albanians!' and 'devils!' and 'off to Siberia!'" Berg said with a knowing smile. "I knew I was right, so I kept quiet. Wasn't that the best approach, Count? 'Hey, are you deaf?' he yelled. I still said nothing. And guess what, Count? The next day there wasn't a word about it in the daily orders. That's what keeping your head gets you. That's how it's done, Count," Berg concluded, lighting his pipe and blowing smoke rings.
"Yes, that was well done," said Rostov with a smile.

But Boris noticed Rostov was gearing up to make fun of Berg and skillfully changed the subject. He asked Rostov to tell them how and where he'd been wounded. This pleased Rostov, and he launched into the story, growing more animated as he went. He described the action at Schon Grabern the way people who've been in battle usually do — not as it actually happened, but as they wished it had, as they'd heard others describe it, as it sounded good. Rostov was an honest young man who would never tell a deliberate lie. He started out intending to describe everything exactly as it occurred, but gradually, involuntarily, inevitably, he slid into invention. If he'd told his listeners the plain truth — listeners who, like him, had heard plenty of battle stories and had a fixed idea of what a cavalry charge should sound like — they either wouldn't have believed him or, worse, would have thought Rostov himself was to blame for things not going the way such stories usually went. He couldn't just say that everyone rode forward at a trot, that he fell off his horse and sprained his arm, and then ran as fast as he could into the woods to escape a Frenchman. Besides, telling the unvarnished truth would have required a deliberate effort of will to describe only what had actually happened. Telling the truth is very hard, and young people are rarely capable of it. His listeners expected to hear how he'd been beside himself with excitement, how he'd charged the enemy like a whirlwind, cut his way through, slashing left and right, how his saber had tasted blood and he'd fallen from exhaustion. And that's what he told them.

In the middle of his story — just as he was saying, "You can't imagine what a strange frenzy comes over you during a charge" — Prince Andrew walked in. Boris had been expecting him. Prince Andrew, who enjoyed helping young men and was flattered to be asked for assistance, was well-disposed toward Boris, who had impressed him the day before, and wanted to help. Having been sent with documents from Kutuzov to the Tsarevich, he'd stopped by to see Boris, hoping to find him alone. When he entered and saw a front-line hussar holding forth about his military exploits — the type of person Prince Andrew couldn't stand — he gave Boris a friendly smile but frowned, half-closing his eyes as he looked at Rostov. He gave a slight, weary bow and sat down on the sofa with an air of languid boredom, clearly regretting that he'd walked in on such company. Rostov flushed when he noticed this, but he didn't care — this was just some stranger. Glancing at Boris, however, he could see that Boris, too, seemed embarrassed by the front-line hussar.

Despite Prince Andrew's unpleasant, mocking tone, and despite the contempt Rostov felt — from his fighting soldier's perspective — for all these little staff adjutants (which the newcomer clearly was), Rostov felt flustered. He blushed and fell silent. Boris asked what news there was from headquarters and what, without being indiscreet, one might learn about their plans.
"We'll probably advance," Bolkonsky replied, evidently reluctant to say more with a stranger present.

Berg seized the opportunity to ask, with elaborate politeness, whether it was true that the forage allowance for company captains would be doubled. Prince Andrew answered with a smile that he couldn't offer an opinion on such an important government matter, and Berg laughed delightedly.
"As for your business," Prince Andrew continued, turning to Boris, "we'll discuss it later." He glanced around at Rostov. "Come see me after the review and we'll see what can be arranged."

Then, looking around the room, Prince Andrew turned to Rostov — whose state of obvious, childish embarrassment, now giving way to anger, he didn't deign to acknowledge — and said: "I believe you were talking about the action at Schon Grabern? Were you there?"
"I was there," Rostov said aggressively, as if meaning to insult the adjutant.
Bolkonsky noticed the hussar's hostile mood, and it amused him. With a slightly condescending smile, he said: "Yes, quite a few stories are circulating about that engagement."

"Yes, stories!" Rostov repeated loudly, his eyes blazing with sudden fury as he looked from Boris to Bolkonsky. "Yes, plenty of stories! But our stories come from men who've actually been under enemy fire! Our stories carry some weight — not like the tales of staff officers who collect medals without doing a thing!"
"Is that what you think I am?" Prince Andrew asked with a calm, notably pleasant smile.
A strange mixture of rage and reluctant respect for this man's composure churned in Rostov at that moment.
"I'm not talking about you," he said. "I don't know you and, frankly, I don't want to. I'm talking about the staff in general."

"Then let me say this," Prince Andrew interrupted, his voice quiet but carrying unmistakable authority. "You clearly want to insult me, and I'll grant you it would be easy enough if you lack basic self-respect. But I'd suggest the time and place are poorly chosen. In a day or two we'll all be engaged in a far greater and more serious contest. Besides, Drubetskoy here — who says he's an old friend of yours — is hardly to blame because you find my face disagreeable. In any case," he added, rising, "you know my name and where to find me. But I want you to understand that I consider neither myself nor you insulted. And as someone older than you, my advice would be to let the whole thing drop. So then — Friday after the review, Drubetskoy, I'll be expecting you. Goodbye!" Prince Andrew bowed to them both and left.

Only after Prince Andrew was gone did Rostov think of what he should have said. And he was even angrier at himself for having failed to say it. He immediately called for his horse and, taking a cold leave of Boris, rode home. Should he ride to headquarters the next day and challenge that arrogant adjutant, or should he just let it go? This question tormented him the entire way. He thought furiously about the pleasure of seeing that small, slight, proud man's fear when facing his pistol — and then felt a surge of surprise, because of all the people he knew, there was no one he'd rather have as a friend than that very adjutant he hated so much.

title: Book Three (1805) — Chapter 8
paragraphs: The day after Rostov's visit to Boris, a review was held of the Austrian and Russian forces — both the fresh troops from Russia and those who had been campaigning under Kutuzov. The two Emperors — the Russian Emperor with his heir the Tsarevich, and the Austrian Emperor with the Archduke — inspected the combined allied army of eighty thousand men.

From early morning, the immaculate troops had been on the move, forming up on the field before the fortress. Thousands of boots and bayonets marched and halted at officers' commands, turned with banners flying, formed up at intervals, and wheeled around similar blocks of infantry in different uniforms. Then came the rhythmic beat of hooves and the jingling of gleaming cavalry in blue, red, and green braided uniforms, led by smartly dressed bandsmen on black, bay, and gray horses. After them, rattling and gleaming, came the artillery — polished cannons quivering on their carriages, trailing the smell of burning match — which rolled between the infantry and cavalry to take up its assigned position. Not just the generals in full-dress uniforms, their waists cinched tight (whether thin or thick), red necks squeezed into stiff collars, wearing sashes and every decoration they owned — not just the polished, pomaded officers — but every single soldier with his freshly washed and shaven face, his weapons cleaned and polished to a shine, every horse groomed until its coat gleamed like satin with each hair of its dampened mane lying perfectly smooth — all of them sensed that this was no small matter but something important and solemn. Every general and every soldier felt his own insignificance, understood that he was merely a drop in that ocean of men, yet at the same time felt his strength as part of that enormous whole.

From early morning, intense effort and activity had been under way, and by ten o'clock everything was in perfect order. The ranks stretched across the vast field. The entire army was arranged in three lines: cavalry in front, artillery behind it, and infantry at the rear.

A gap like a street was left between each pair of lines. The three parts of the army were clearly distinct: Kutuzov's battle-tested troops (with the Pavlograds on the right flank of the front line), the recently arrived forces from Russia — both Guards and line regiments — and the Austrian troops. But they all stood in the same formation, under a single command, in uniform order.
An excited whisper rippled through the ranks like wind through leaves: "They're coming! They're coming!" Anxious voices rang out, and a final wave of preparation swept through all the troops.

A group appeared approaching from the direction of Olmutz. And at that moment, though the day was calm, a light breeze passed over the army, just barely stirring the streamers on the lances and ruffling the unfurled standards against their staffs. It was as if the army itself, with that slight flutter, was expressing its joy at the Emperors' approach. A single voice rang out: "Eyes front!" Then, like roosters crowing at dawn, the command was repeated from all directions, and everything fell silent.

In the deathly stillness, only the tramping of horses could be heard. This was the Emperors' entourage. They rode up to the flank, and the trumpets of the first cavalry regiment played the general march. It seemed as though the trumpeters weren't playing at all — as though the army itself, overjoyed at the Emperors' approach, had spontaneously burst into music. Through these sounds, only one voice could be clearly heard: the young, warm voice of Emperor Alexander. He spoke the words of greeting, and the first regiment roared "Hurrah!" so thunderously, so continuously, so joyfully that the soldiers themselves were awed by their own numbers and the immensity of their combined power.

Rostov, standing in the front ranks of Kutuzov's army — which the Tsar approached first — felt exactly what every other man in that army felt: a sense of losing himself, a proud awareness of collective might, and a passionate devotion to the man who had caused this triumph.

He felt that a single word from that man would send this entire vast mass — and he himself, an insignificant speck within it — through fire and water, to commit any act, to die, or to perform the greatest heroism. And so he couldn't help trembling, his heart stopping at the thought that the word might come at any moment.

"Hurrah! Hurrah! Hurrah!" roared from every side as regiment after regiment greeted the Tsar with the strains of the march, then another "Hurrah!" The general march, then "Hurrah! Hurrah!" — growing ever louder and fuller, merging into a single deafening roar.

Until the Tsar reached a given regiment, it stood in silence and stillness like a lifeless body. But the moment he drew near, it burst to life, its thunder joining the roar of the whole line he had already passed. Through the terrible, deafening wall of sound, amid the motionless square formations standing rigid as stone, hundreds of riders in the imperial retinue moved casually but gracefully, and above all freely. And at the head of them rode two men — the Emperors. On them was focused the total, intense, passionate attention of that entire mass of humanity.
The handsome young Emperor Alexander, wearing the uniform of the Horse Guards and a cocked hat with its peaks front and back, drew every eye with his pleasant face and clear, resonant voice.

Rostov was not far from the trumpeters, and with his sharp eyesight he recognized the Tsar and watched his approach. When Alexander was about twenty paces away and Nicholas could clearly make out every feature of his handsome, happy young face, he was swept by a feeling of tenderness and rapture unlike anything he had ever known. Every expression, every movement of the Tsar's seemed enchanting to him.
As the Tsar stopped in front of the Pavlograds, he said something in French to the Austrian Emperor and smiled.

Seeing that smile, Rostov couldn't help smiling himself, feeling an even stronger surge of love for his sovereign. He longed to express that love somehow, and knowing it was impossible, he was ready to weep. The Tsar called the regiment's colonel over and said a few words to him.
"Oh God, what would happen to me if the Emperor spoke to me?" Rostov thought. "I would die of happiness!"

The Tsar addressed the officers as well: "I thank you all, gentlemen. I thank you with my whole heart." To Rostov, every word sounded like a voice from heaven. How gladly he would have died on the spot for his Tsar!
"You have earned the St. George's standards and will prove worthy of them."
"Oh, to die, to die for him," Rostov thought.
The Tsar said something more that Rostov couldn't hear, and the soldiers, straining their lungs, shouted "Hurrah!"
Rostov too, bending over his saddle, bellowed "Hurrah!" with every ounce of strength, feeling he could injure himself with that shout if it meant fully expressing his devotion.
The Tsar paused for a few moments in front of the hussars, as if unsure of something.
"How can the Emperor be uncertain?" Rostov thought — but even this hesitation seemed majestic and enchanting, like everything else the Tsar did.

The hesitation lasted only an instant. The Tsar's foot, in the narrow, pointed boot that was fashionable at the time, touched the flank of the bob-tailed bay mare he rode. His white-gloved hand gathered the reins, and he moved off, accompanied by an irregularly swaying crowd of aides-de-camp. Farther and farther he rode, stopping at other regiments, until finally only his white plumes were visible to Rostov among the entourage surrounding the Emperors.

Among the riders in the retinue, Rostov spotted Bolkonsky, sitting his horse with casual indifference. He remembered their clash the day before, and the question arose: should he challenge Bolkonsky or not? "Of course not!" he thought now. "How can I even consider it at a moment like this? At a time of such love, such ecstasy, such self-sacrifice, what do any of our petty quarrels and insults matter? I love and forgive everyone now."

When the Emperor had passed nearly all the regiments, the troops began the ceremonial march past him. Rostov rode by on Bedouin — the horse he'd recently bought from Denisov — at the rear of his squadron, which meant he was riding alone and in full view of the Emperor.

As he approached, Rostov — an excellent horseman — spurred Bedouin twice and put him into the showy, collected trot the horse adopted when excited. With his foaming muzzle tucked to his chest and tail streaming out behind him, Bedouin seemed to feel the Emperor's gaze upon him too. He moved magnificently, lifting his hooves high in an elegant, floating action, as if barely touching the ground.

Rostov himself, legs pressed well back, stomach drawn in, feeling himself and his horse as one, rode past the Emperor with a fierce but blissful expression on his face — "like a real devil," as Denisov would have put it.
"Fine fellows, the Pavlograds!" the Emperor remarked.
"My God, how happy I would be if he ordered me to ride into fire this very second!" Rostov thought.

When the review was over, the newly arrived officers and Kutuzov's veterans alike gathered in groups to discuss the awards, the Austrian uniforms and formations, and Bonaparte — and how badly things would go for him now, especially once the Essen corps arrived and Prussia joined their side.
But in every group, the main topic of conversation was Emperor Alexander. Every word he'd spoken, every gesture he'd made was described with adoration.

Everyone shared a single wish: to advance against the enemy as soon as possible under the Emperor's personal command. With the Emperor himself leading them, they could not possibly lose to anyone — so believed Rostov and most of the officers after the review.
All of them felt more confident of victory than they would have after winning two actual battles.

title: Book Three (1805) — Chapter 9
paragraphs: The day after the review, Boris put on his best uniform and, with his roommate Berg's earnest good wishes, rode to Olmutz to see Bolkonsky. He wanted to take advantage of Prince Andrew's friendliness and secure the best position he could — ideally as adjutant to some important figure, which struck him as the most desirable role in the army. "It's all very well for Rostov, whose father sends him ten thousand rubles at a time, to talk about refusing to grovel and not being anyone's lackey," he reflected, "but I have nothing but my wits and have to build a career. I can't afford to pass up opportunities — I have to seize them."

He didn't find Prince Andrew in Olmutz that day, but the sight of the town — with its concentration of headquarters staff, diplomatic corps, and the two Emperors and their households, courts, and retinues — only strengthened his determination to break into that elite world.

He didn't know anyone there, and despite his smart Guards uniform, all these exalted figures passing through the streets in elegant carriages — festooned with plumes, ribbons, and medals, courtiers and military officers alike — seemed so infinitely above him, a lowly Guards lieutenant, that they not only didn't want to acknowledge his existence but simply couldn't. At the commander-in-chief's quarters, where he asked for Bolkonsky, all the adjutants and even the orderlies looked at him as though trying to communicate that officers like him showed up constantly and everyone was thoroughly sick of them. Despite this — or rather, because of it — the next day, November 15th, he returned to Olmutz after dinner and went to the house Kutuzov was occupying. He asked for Bolkonsky. Prince Andrew was in, and Boris was led into a large hall that had probably once been used for dancing but now held five beds along with an assortment of furniture — a table, chairs, and a clavichord. One adjutant, nearest the door, sat at the table in a Persian dressing gown, writing. Another — the red-faced, heavyset Nesvitsky — lay on a bed with his hands behind his head, laughing with an officer who had sat down next to him. A third was playing a Viennese waltz on the clavichord while a fourth lay draped across it, singing along. Bolkonsky was not among them. None of these gentlemen shifted when Boris entered. The one who was writing, and to whom Boris spoke, turned around irritably and told him that Bolkonsky was on duty and that if he wanted to see him, he should go through the door on the left into the reception room. Boris thanked him and went through. In the reception room he found about ten officers and generals.

When Boris entered, Prince Andrew — his eyes half-closed with that look of polite exhaustion that clearly says "If this weren't my duty, I wouldn't waste a moment talking to you" — was listening to an old Russian general covered in decorations. The general stood ramrod straight, almost on tiptoe, a soldier's obsequious expression on his purple face, as he reported something.

"Very well, then — please wait," Prince Andrew said to the general in Russian, using the French intonation he adopted when he wanted to convey disdain. Noticing Boris, he paid no further attention to the general — who followed after him, begging to be heard — and turned to Boris with a warm smile.

At that moment, Boris understood clearly what he had only sensed before: that in the army, beyond the official chain of command and regulations he'd learned in the regiment, there existed another, far more important hierarchy — an unwritten one that made this rigid, purple-faced general wait respectfully while Captain Prince Andrew chose, at his leisure, to chat with Lieutenant Drubetskoy. More than ever, Boris resolved to serve according to this unwritten code rather than the official one. He realized that simply by being recommended to Prince Andrew, he had already risen above the general who, at the front, had the power to crush him — a mere Guards lieutenant. Prince Andrew came up and took his hand.
"I'm really sorry you didn't find me yesterday. I was running around with Germans all day. We went with Weyrother to survey the battle plans. When Germans get precise, there's no end to it!"
Boris smiled as if he understood perfectly what Prince Andrew was referring to. But it was the first time he had ever heard Weyrother's name or even the term "dispositions."
"Well, my dear fellow, so you still want to be an adjutant? I've been thinking about you."

"Yes, I was thinking" — for some reason Boris couldn't help blushing — "of asking the commander-in-chief directly. He's received a letter from Prince Kuragin about me. I just wanted to ask because I'm afraid the Guards won't see any action," he added, almost apologetically.
"All right, all right. We'll talk it over," Prince Andrew replied. "Just let me finish with this gentleman's business, and then I'm all yours."

While Prince Andrew went to deal with the purple-faced general, that officer — clearly not sharing Boris's appreciation for the unwritten rules of military hierarchy — stared so hard at the presumptuous lieutenant who had interrupted his audience that Boris felt distinctly uncomfortable. He turned away and waited impatiently for Prince Andrew to return from the commander-in-chief's room.

"You see, my dear fellow, I've been thinking about your situation," Prince Andrew said when they'd gone into the big room with the clavichord. "There's no point in going to the commander-in-chief. He'd say a lot of nice things, invite you to dinner" — "That wouldn't be so bad, according to the unwritten code," Boris thought — "but nothing would actually come of it. There'll soon be a whole battalion of us aides-de-camp and adjutants! But here's what we'll do: I have a good friend, an adjutant general and excellent fellow — Prince Dolgorukov. What you may not realize is that right now, Kutuzov and his entire staff — all of us — count for nothing. Everything revolves around the Emperor. So we'll go to Dolgorukov. I need to see him anyway, and I've already mentioned you. We'll see if he can take you onto his own staff or place you somewhere closer to the center of things."

Prince Andrew always became particularly energetic when he had the chance to guide a young man and help him advance in the world. By helping others in a way he was too proud to seek for himself, he maintained connections with the circles that dispensed success and power — circles that attracted him. He took up Boris's cause eagerly and went with him to see Dolgorukov.
It was late evening when they arrived at the palace in Olmutz occupied by the Emperors and their entourages.

That same day, a council of war had been held. All the members of the Austrian War Council and both Emperors had attended. At this council, overriding the views of the old generals — Kutuzov and Prince Schwarzenberg — it had been decided to advance immediately and engage Bonaparte in battle. The council had just ended when Prince Andrew and Boris arrived at the palace to find Dolgorukov. Everyone at headquarters was still under the spell of that day's debate, in which the war party had triumphed. The voices of those who had counseled delay and argued for waiting had been so thoroughly silenced, their objections so conclusively demolished with evidence of the benefits of attacking, that the subject of the council — the coming battle and its inevitable victory — no longer felt like something in the future but like something already accomplished. All the advantages were on their side. Their enormous forces, clearly superior to Napoleon's, were concentrated in one place. The troops, inspired by the presence of both Emperors, were hungry for action. The strategic ground where operations would unfold was known in minute detail to the Austrian General Weyrother. By a fortunate coincidence, the Austrian army had maneuvered the previous year on the very same fields where the French would now have to be fought. Every feature of the surrounding terrain was mapped and documented in exhaustive detail. And Bonaparte, clearly weakened, was making no moves.

Dolgorukov — one of the most passionate advocates of attacking — had just come from the council, exhausted but excited and proud of the victory he'd helped win. Prince Andrew introduced his protege, but Prince Dolgorukov, politely and firmly shaking Boris's hand, said nothing to him. Clearly unable to contain the thoughts filling his mind, he turned to Prince Andrew and spoke in French.

"Ah, my dear fellow, what a victory we've won! God grant that the battle it leads to will be just as successful! But I must confess, dear friend" — he spoke rapidly and eagerly — "I've been unfair to the Austrians, especially to Weyrother. What precision, what thoroughness, what mastery of the terrain, what foresight for every eventuality — even the smallest detail! No, my dear fellow, no conditions more favorable than the ones we have now could possibly be devised. Austrian precision combined with Russian courage — what more could anyone ask for?"
"So the attack has been definitely decided on?" Bolkonsky asked.

"And you know what, my dear fellow — it seems to me Bonaparte has completely lost his footing. Did you know a letter arrived from him today addressed to the Emperor?" Dolgorukov said with a meaningful smile.
"Is that so? What did he say?" Bolkonsky asked.

"What can he say? Just stalling for time with a lot of diplomatic noise. I'm telling you — he's in our hands. That's a fact! But the funniest part," he continued with a sudden, good-natured laugh, "was that we couldn't figure out how to address the reply! We couldn't call him 'Consul,' and obviously not 'Emperor' — so it seemed to me we should just write 'General Bonaparte.'"
"But there's quite a gap between refusing to call him Emperor and addressing him as General Bonaparte," Bolkonsky observed.
"Exactly!" Dolgorukov broke in, laughing. "You know Bilibin — he's very clever. He suggested addressing it to 'The Usurper and Enemy of Mankind.'"
Dolgorukov laughed heartily.
"That's all?" Bolkonsky said.
"Still, it was Bilibin who came up with the proper form. He really is a brilliant fellow."
"What was it?"
"'To the Head of the French Government'... Au chef du gouvernement français," Dolgorukov said with an air of grave satisfaction. "Good, don't you think?"
"Yes, but he'll be extremely displeased," Bolkonsky said.

"Oh, absolutely! My brother knows him — he's dined with the present Emperor more than once in Paris — and he says he's never encountered a more cunning or more subtle diplomat. You know the type: French shrewdness combined with Italian theatrics. Have you heard the story about him and Count Markov? Markov was the only man who knew how to handle him. You know the handkerchief anecdote? It's wonderful!"

And the talkative Dolgorukov, turning from Boris to Prince Andrew and back, told how Bonaparte — wanting to test Markov, the Russian ambassador — had deliberately dropped a handkerchief in front of him and stood waiting, clearly expecting Markov to pick it up. Instead, Markov immediately dropped his own handkerchief beside it and picked up his own, leaving Bonaparte's on the floor.

"Wonderful!" Bolkonsky said. "But I've come to you, Prince, as a petitioner on behalf of this young man. You see..." But before Prince Andrew could finish, an aide-de-camp came in to summon Dolgorukov to the Emperor.

"Oh, what a nuisance," said Dolgorukov, jumping up and shaking hands with both Prince Andrew and Boris. "You know I'd be delighted to do everything I can for you and for this fine young man." He pressed Boris's hand again with an expression of genuine, warmhearted sincerity. "But you see... another time!"

Boris was thrilled at finding himself so close to the levers of power. He was acutely aware that here, at this very spot, he was in contact with the hidden springs that set in motion the enormous forces in which he — back in his regiment — felt himself to be a tiny, obedient, insignificant particle. They followed Prince Dolgorukov into the corridor and nearly collided with a short man in civilian clothes coming out of the door to the Emperor's room. The man had a shrewd face and a sharply projecting jaw that, without spoiling his features, gave him a look of particular alertness and cunning. He nodded to Dolgorukov like an old friend and fixed Prince Andrew with a cool, penetrating stare, walking straight toward him as if expecting a bow or for him to step aside. Prince Andrew did neither. A flash of hostility crossed his face, and the other man turned away and continued down the corridor.
"Who was that?" Boris asked.

"He is one of the most remarkable men of our time — but to me, one of the most disagreeable: the Minister of Foreign Affairs, Prince Adam Czartoryski... It is men like him who decide the fate of nations," Bolkonsky added with a sigh he couldn't suppress as they walked out of the palace.
The next day, the army began its campaign, and right up until the Battle of Austerlitz, Boris had no chance to see either Prince Andrew or Dolgorukov again. He remained with the Ismaylov regiment.

title: Book Three (1805) — Chapter 10
paragraphs: At dawn on November 16th, Denisov's squadron — the one in which Nicholas Rostov served, part of Prince Bagration's detachment — moved out from where it had spent the night and advanced into action as planned. After marching behind other columns for about two-thirds of a mile, they were stopped on the main road. Rostov watched the Cossacks pass by, then the first and second squadrons of hussars, then infantry battalions and artillery, and finally Generals Bagration and Dolgorukov riding past with their adjutants. All the fear he'd felt before battle, all his inner struggle to conquer that fear, all his dreams of proving himself a true hussar — it had all been for nothing. Their squadron was held in reserve, and Nicholas Rostov spent the day in a miserable, frustrated mood. At nine in the morning he heard gunfire ahead and shouts of "Hurrah!" and saw wounded men being carried back (not many of them), and eventually watched as a whole detachment of French cavalry was brought in under Cossack escort. The engagement was clearly over — small but successful. The men and officers returning spoke of a brilliant victory, the capture of the town of Wischau, and the seizure of an entire French squadron. The day was bright and sunny after a sharp overnight frost, and the cheerful autumn light matched the mood of victory, which was conveyed not just by the stories of those who had fought, but by the joyful expressions on the faces of soldiers, officers, generals, and adjutants passing Rostov in both directions. And Nicholas, who had suffered all the dread of anticipation for nothing and spent that fine day doing nothing, felt even more depressed.
"Come here, Rostov. Let's drink to drown our sorrows!" shouted Denisov, who had settled by the roadside with a flask and some food.
The officers gathered around Denisov's canteen, eating and talking.
"Look! They're bringing in another one!" cried one of the officers, pointing at a captured French dragoon being led in on foot by two Cossacks.
One of the Cossacks was leading a fine, large French horse by the bridle — taken from the prisoner.
"Sell us that horse!" Denisov called out to the Cossacks.
"If you like, your honor!"

The officers got up and gathered around the Cossacks and their prisoner. The French dragoon was a young man from Alsace who spoke French with a German accent. He was breathless with agitation, his face was red, and as soon as he heard French being spoken he started talking rapidly to the officers, turning from one to another. He said he wouldn't have been captured — it wasn't his fault but the corporal's, who had sent him to fetch some horse blankets even though he'd warned him the Russians were there. And with every other sentence he added: "But don't hurt my little horse!" and stroked the animal. It was obvious he hadn't fully grasped his situation. One moment he was apologizing for getting captured, the next he was acting as if he were standing before his own commanding officers, insisting on his military discipline and dedication. He brought with him into the Russian rearguard all the freshness and atmosphere of the French army, which felt completely foreign to them.
The Cossacks sold the horse for two gold pieces, and Rostov, now the richest officer in the group after receiving his money, bought it.
"But don't hurt my little horse!" said the Alsatian good-naturedly to Rostov when the animal was handed over to the hussar.
Rostov smiled reassuringly at the dragoon and gave him money.
"Move along! Move along!" said the Cossack, tapping the prisoner's arm to get him walking.
"The Emperor! The Emperor!" The cry suddenly ran through the hussars.

Everyone began running about and getting into position, and Rostov saw several riders approaching from up the road behind him, white plumes in their hats. In an instant every man was in his place, waiting.

Rostov didn't know or remember how he ran to his position and mounted his horse. Instantly his regret at missing the action was gone, his dreary mood among people he was tired of had vanished, and every thought of himself had disappeared. He was filled with happiness at being near the Emperor. He felt this closeness alone made up for the entire wasted day. He was as happy as a lover at the long-awaited moment of reunion. Not daring to look around, and without looking around, he was ecstatically aware of the Emperor's approach. He sensed it not just from the sound of approaching hooves but because as the Emperor drew nearer, everything around him grew brighter, more joyful, more meaningful, more festive. That sun, radiating its mild and majestic light, came closer and closer, and already Rostov felt himself wrapped in its glow. He heard the Emperor's voice — that kind, calm, majestic voice that was at the same time so simple! And as if in harmony with Rostov's feelings, a deathlike stillness fell, broken only by the Emperor's words.
"The Pavlograd hussars?" he asked.
"The reserves, sire!" replied a voice — a very human one compared to the voice that had said "The Pavlograd hussars?"

The Emperor drew level with Rostov and stopped. Alexander's face was even more beautiful than it had been three days earlier at the review. It glowed with such cheerfulness and youth, such innocent youthfulness, that it resembled a lively fourteen-year-old boy — and yet it was the face of the Emperor himself. While casually surveying the squadron, his eyes met Rostov's and rested on them for no more than two seconds. Whether or not the Emperor understood what was happening in Rostov's heart (it seemed to Rostov that he understood everything), his light-blue eyes gazed into Rostov's face for about two seconds. A gentle, soft light poured from them. Then suddenly he raised his eyebrows, touched his horse sharply with his left foot, and galloped on.

The young Emperor had been unable to resist his desire to be present at the battle, and despite the objections of his courtiers, had left the third column at noon and galloped toward the front lines. Before he reached the hussars, several adjutants had already met him with news of the successful action.

This battle — which amounted to the capture of a French squadron — was portrayed as a brilliant victory over the French, and so the Emperor and the entire army, especially while smoke still hung over the battlefield, believed the French had been defeated and were retreating against their will. A few minutes after the Emperor rode past, the Pavlograd division was ordered to advance. In Wischau itself, a small German town, Rostov saw the Emperor again. In the market square, where there had been fairly heavy fighting before the Emperor arrived, several dead and wounded soldiers lay where they had fallen — there hadn't been time to move them. The Emperor, surrounded by his officers and courtiers, was riding a bob-tailed chestnut mare — a different horse from the one at the review — and leaning to one side, he gracefully held a gold lorgnette to his eyes and looked down at a soldier lying face-down, blood on his bare head. The wounded man was so dirty, rough, and disfigured that his closeness to the Emperor shocked Rostov. Rostov saw how the Emperor's rounded shoulders shuddered as though a chill ran through them, how his left foot began involuntarily tapping the horse's side with the spur, and how the well-trained horse glanced around unconcerned and didn't move. An adjutant dismounted and lifted the soldier under the arms to place him on a stretcher that had been brought up. The soldier groaned.
"Gently, gently! Can't you do it more carefully?" said the Emperor, apparently suffering more than the dying soldier himself, and he rode away.
Rostov saw tears filling the Emperor's eyes and heard him say to Czartoryski as he rode off: "What a terrible thing war is — what a terrible thing!"

The vanguard troops were positioned in front of Wischau, within sight of the enemy's lines, which had given ground all day at the slightest exchange of fire. The Emperor's gratitude was announced to the vanguard, rewards were promised, and the men received a double ration of vodka. The campfires crackled and the soldiers' songs rang out even louder than the night before. Denisov was celebrating his promotion to major, and Rostov, who had already drunk plenty, proposed a toast to the Emperor at the end of the feast. "Not 'our Sovereign, the Emperor,' the way they say it at official dinners," he said, "but to the health of our Sovereign — that good, wonderful, and great man! Let's drink to his health and to the certain defeat of the French!"

"If we fought the way we did before," he continued, "not letting the French through, like at Schon Grabern — what won't we do now that he himself is leading us? We'll all gladly die for him! Isn't that right, gentlemen? Maybe I'm not saying this perfectly — I've had a lot to drink — but that's how I feel, and I know you feel the same! To the health of Alexander the First! Hurrah!"
"Hurrah!" rang out the enthusiastic voices of the officers.
And the old cavalry captain Kirsten shouted just as enthusiastically and just as sincerely as the twenty-year-old Rostov.

When the officers had drained and smashed their glasses, Kirsten filled new ones and, in his shirtsleeves and breeches, walked glass in hand to the soldiers' bonfires. With his long gray mustache and his white chest showing through his open shirt, he stood in a grand pose by the firelight, waving his raised arm.
"Boys! To our Sovereign, the Emperor, and victory over our enemies! Hurrah!" he bellowed in his bold, old hussar's baritone.
The hussars crowded around and responded with hearty, loud cheers.
Late that night, after everyone had gone their separate ways, Denisov patted his favorite, Rostov, on the shoulder with his short hand.
"Since there's no one to fall in love with on campaign, he's gone and fallen in love with the Tsar," he said.
"Denisov, don't joke about it!" cried Rostov. "It's such an elevated, beautiful feeling, such a..."
"I believe you, I believe you, my friend, and I share it and approve..."
"No, you don't understand!"

And Rostov got up and wandered among the campfires, dreaming of what happiness it would be to die — not saving the Emperor's life (he didn't even dare dream of that), but simply to die before his eyes. He truly was in love with the Tsar, with the glory of Russian arms, and with the hope of future victory. And he wasn't the only one who felt this way during those memorable days before the battle of Austerlitz: nine-tenths of the men in the Russian army were then in love, though less ecstatically, with their Tsar and the glory of Russian arms.

title: Book Three (1805) — Chapter 11
paragraphs: The next day the Emperor stayed in Wischau, and his physician Villier was called in repeatedly. At headquarters and among the nearby troops, word spread that the Emperor was unwell. He had eaten nothing and slept badly, according to those around him. The cause of his illness was the powerful impression the sight of the dead and wounded had made on his sensitive nature.

At dawn on the seventeenth, a French officer carrying a flag of truce and requesting an audience with the Russian Emperor was brought into Wischau from the outposts. The officer was Savary. The Emperor had only just fallen asleep, so Savary had to wait. At noon he was admitted to see the Emperor, and an hour later he rode off with Prince Dolgorukov toward the French army's forward positions.

It was rumored that Savary had been sent to propose a meeting between Alexander and Napoleon. To the joy and pride of the entire army, a personal meeting was refused, and instead of the Emperor himself, Prince Dolgorukov — the victor at Wischau — was sent with Savary to negotiate with Napoleon, in case these negotiations reflected a genuine desire for peace.
Toward evening Dolgorukov returned, went straight to the Tsar, and remained alone with him for a long time.

On November 18th and 19th, the army advanced two days' march, and the enemy's outposts retreated after brief exchanges of fire. In the highest military circles, from midday on the 19th, a frantic, excited flurry of activity began that lasted until the morning of the 20th, when the famous battle of Austerlitz was fought.

Until midday on the 19th, the activity — the urgent conversations, the rushing back and forth, the dispatching of adjutants — was confined to the Emperor's headquarters. But that afternoon it reached Kutuzov's headquarters and the staffs of the column commanders. By evening the adjutants had carried it to every corner of the army, and during the night of the 19th-20th, the entire force of eighty thousand allied troops rose from their bivouacs to a hum of voices, and the army surged and set off in one enormous mass six miles long.

The concentrated activity that had begun at the Emperor's headquarters that morning and set the whole movement in motion was like the first turn of the main wheel in a great tower clock. One wheel slowly began to move, then another, then a third, and soon wheels were spinning faster and faster, levers and gears engaged, chimes began to play, figures popped out, and the hands advanced with steady regularity — all as a result of that initial motion.

Just as in a clock's mechanism, so in the mechanism of the military machine: once an impulse is given, it leads inevitably to the final result. And just as the untouched parts of a clock sit completely still until the motion reaches them — wheels that could remain idle for a hundred years — so it is in an army. But the moment comes when the lever catches, and that dormant wheel begins to creak and joins the common motion, the ultimate result and purpose of which are beyond its comprehension.

Just as in a clock the result of the complicated motion of countless wheels and pulleys is simply the slow, steady movement of the hands showing the time, so the result of all the complicated human activities of 160,000 Russians and French — all their passions, desires, remorse, humiliation, suffering, bursts of pride, fear, and enthusiasm — was nothing more than the loss of the battle of Austerlitz, the so-called Battle of the Three Emperors — that is, a slow movement of the hand on the dial of human history.
Prince Andrew was on duty that day and in constant attendance on the commander in chief.
At six in the evening, Kutuzov went to the Emperor's headquarters, and after spending only a short time with the Tsar, went to see the grand marshal of the court, Count Tolstoy.

Bolkonsky seized the opportunity to visit Dolgorukov and get some details about the coming battle. He sensed that Kutuzov was upset and dissatisfied about something, and also that the people at the Emperor's headquarters were dissatisfied with Kutuzov — and that everyone there spoke with the air of people who know something others don't. So he wanted to talk to Dolgorukov.
"Well, how are you, my dear fellow?" said Dolgorukov, who was sitting having tea with Bilibin. "The celebration is tomorrow. How's your old man? Out of sorts?"
"I wouldn't say out of sorts, but I get the feeling he'd like to be heard."
"But they did hear him at the council of war, and they'll hear him again when he talks sense. But to hesitate and wait when Bonaparte fears nothing more than a full-scale battle — that's impossible."
"Yes, you've seen him?" said Prince Andrew. "So what is Bonaparte like? What impression did he make on you?"

"Yes, I saw him, and I'm convinced he fears nothing more than a general engagement," Dolgorukov repeated, clearly prizing this conclusion he'd drawn from his meeting with Napoleon. "If he weren't afraid of battle, why would he have requested that meeting? Why negotiate? And above all, why retreat — when retreating goes completely against his usual way of making war? Believe me, he's afraid. Afraid of a full battle. His time has come! Mark my words!"
"But tell me, what is he actually like?" Prince Andrew asked again.

"He's a man in a gray overcoat who very much wanted me to call him 'Your Majesty' but was annoyed to get no such title from me. That's what he is, nothing more," replied Dolgorukov, glancing at Bilibin with a smile.

"Despite my great respect for old Kutuzov," he went on, "we'd be fools to sit around waiting and give Napoleon a chance to escape or trick us, now that we clearly have him in our grasp! No, we must remember Suvorov's rule: don't put yourself in a position to be attacked — attack first. Believe me, in war the energy of young men often shows the way better than all the experience of old procrastinators."
"But in what position are we going to attack him? I was at the outposts today and it's impossible to determine where his main forces are," said Prince Andrew.
He wanted to explain to Dolgorukov a plan of attack he had worked out himself.
"Oh, that doesn't matter at all," Dolgorukov said quickly, and standing up he spread a map on the table. "Every possibility has been anticipated. If he's positioned in front of Brunn..."
And Prince Dolgorukov rapidly but unclearly explained Weyrother's plan for a flanking maneuver.

Prince Andrew began to respond and present his own plan, which might have been just as good as Weyrother's, except that Weyrother's had the disadvantage of already being approved. As soon as Prince Andrew started pointing out the flaws in Weyrother's plan and the strengths of his own, Dolgorukov stopped listening and stared absently — not at the map, but at Prince Andrew's face.
"There'll be a council of war at Kutuzov's tonight — you can present all this there," Dolgorukov remarked.
"I will," said Prince Andrew, stepping back from the map.

"Whatever are you two getting worked up about, gentlemen?" said Bilibin, who had been listening to their conversation with an amused smile and was now clearly ready with a witticism. "Whether tomorrow brings victory or defeat, the glory of Russian arms is assured. Aside from your Kutuzov, there isn't a single Russian commanding a column! The commanders are: Herr General Wimpfen, Count Langeron, Prince Lichtenstein, Prince Hohenlohe, and finally Prshprsh — and so on, all those Polish names."
"Quiet, you troublemaker!" said Dolgorukov. "That's not true. There are now two Russians: Miloradovich and Dokhturov. And there'd be a third — Count Arakcheev — if his nerves weren't too fragile."
"Anyway, I think General Kutuzov has come out," said Prince Andrew. "I wish you good luck and success, gentlemen!" he added, and left after shaking hands with Dolgorukov and Bilibin.
On the way back, Prince Andrew couldn't stop himself from asking Kutuzov, who was sitting silently beside him, what he thought about tomorrow's battle.

Kutuzov looked sternly at his adjutant and, after a pause, replied: "I think the battle will be lost, and I said as much to Count Tolstoy. I asked him to tell the Emperor. And do you know what he answered? 'My dear general, I'm busy with rice and cutlets — you look after military matters yourself!' Yes... That was the answer I got!"

title: Book Three (1805) — Chapter 13
paragraphs: That same night, Rostov was on skirmish duty with a platoon, positioned ahead of Bagration's detachment. His hussars were stationed along the line in pairs, and he rode back and forth trying to fight off the drowsiness that kept overcoming him. Behind him stretched an enormous space where the army's campfires glowed dimly through the fog; ahead was nothing but misty darkness. Rostov strained to see into that foggy distance but could make out nothing: now something seemed to gleam gray, now something looked black, now tiny lights appeared to flicker where the enemy should be, then he thought it might just be his own eyes playing tricks. His eyelids kept drooping, and in his half-dreams he saw the Emperor, then Denisov, then memories of Moscow — and then he'd jerk his eyes open again to see the head and ears of his horse right in front of him, and sometimes, when he rode within six paces, the dark shapes of hussars nearby. But in the distance, the same misty darkness remained. "Why not?" thought Rostov. "It could easily happen. The Emperor might come across me and give me an order, just like he would any other officer. He'd say: 'Go find out what's out there.' There are plenty of stories about him noticing an officer by chance and taking him onto his personal staff. What if he gave me a place at his side? Oh, how I would protect him, how I would tell him the truth, how I would expose the people deceiving him!" And to make his devoted love for the sovereign feel more vivid, Rostov imagined an enemy or a treacherous German whom he would not only kill with pleasure but slap across the face right in front of the Emperor. Suddenly a distant shout jerked him awake. He started and opened his eyes.

"Where am I? Oh, right — the skirmish line. Password and countersign: shaft, Olmutz. What a shame our squadron's in reserve tomorrow," he thought. "I'll ask for leave to go to the front. This might be my only chance to see the Emperor. It won't be long until my duty's over. I'll make one more round, and when I get back I'll go to the general and ask." He adjusted himself in the saddle and urged his horse forward to ride another circuit past his hussars. It seemed to him that the sky was growing lighter. To the left he could see an illuminated slope, and facing it a dark hill that looked steep as a wall. On this hill there was a white patch that Rostov couldn't identify — was it a moonlit clearing in the woods, unmelted snow, or some white buildings? He even thought he saw something move on that white spot. "Probably snow... a spot... a patch — une tache," he thought. "Wait... it's not a patch... Natasha... my sister, those dark eyes... Na-tasha... (Won't she be amazed when I tell her I saw the Emperor?) Natasha... take my sabretache..." — "Keep to the right, your honor, there are bushes here," came the voice of a hussar he was riding past, already half asleep. Rostov lifted his head, which had drooped almost to his horse's mane, and pulled up beside the hussar. He was surrendering to an irresistible, youthful, childlike drowsiness. "But what was I thinking about? I mustn't forget. How am I going to speak to the Emperor? No, that's not it — that's tomorrow. Oh yes! Natasha... sabretache... saber them... Whom? The hussars... Ah, the hussars with their mustaches. Down Tverskaya Street rode the hussar with the mustache... I was thinking about him too, right across from Guryev's house... Old Guryev... Oh, but Denisov's a wonderful fellow. But that's all nonsense. The main thing is that the Emperor is here. The way he looked at me and wanted to say something but didn't dare... No, it was I who didn't dare. But that's all nonsense — the main thing is not to forget the important thought I was having. Yes, Na-tasha, sabretache, oh yes, yes! That's right!" And his head sank to his horse's neck once more. Suddenly he thought he was being shot at. "What? What? What?... Cut them down! What?" said Rostov, jolting awake. The moment he opened his eyes, he heard from ahead — from the enemy's direction — the long, drawn-out shouts of thousands of voices. His horse and the hussar's horse beside him pricked up their ears at the sound. Over where the shouting came from, a fire flared up and then went out, then another, and then all along the French line on the hill, fires blazed up one after another and the shouting grew louder and louder. Rostov could hear French words but couldn't make them out. The roar of so many voices was too great; all he could distinguish was "ahahah!" and "rrrr!"
"What's going on? What do you think that is?" said Rostov to the hussar beside him. "That must be the enemy's camp!"
The hussar didn't reply.
"Well? Don't you hear it?" Rostov asked again, after waiting for an answer.
"Who can say, your honor?" the hussar replied reluctantly.
"From the direction, it has to be the enemy," Rostov repeated.
"Maybe it is, maybe it's nothing," the hussar muttered. "It's dark... Steady!" he called to his restless horse.

Rostov's horse was getting agitated too, pawing at the frozen ground, pricking its ears at the noise, and staring toward the lights. The shouting grew even louder, merging into a roar that only an army of several thousand men could produce. The lights spread farther along what was probably the French camp's line. Rostov no longer felt sleepy. The jubilant, triumphant shouting from the enemy camp had an electrifying effect on him. "Long live the Emperor! The Emperor!" — he could now hear the words distinctly.
"They can't be far away — probably just beyond the stream," he said to the hussar beside him.

The hussar only sighed, said nothing, and coughed irritably. The sound of hooves approaching at a trot along the line of hussars reached them, and out of the foggy darkness the figure of a hussar sergeant appeared, looming as large as an elephant.
"Your honor, the generals!" said the sergeant, riding up to Rostov.

Rostov, still glancing back toward the fires and the shouting, rode with the sergeant to meet some mounted men coming along the line. One of them was on a white horse. It was Prince Bagration and Prince Dolgorukov, with their adjutants, who had come to see the strange spectacle of lights and shouts from the enemy camp for themselves. Rostov rode up to Bagration, made his report, and then joined the adjutants listening to the generals' conversation.
"Believe me," said Prince Dolgorukov, turning to Bagration, "it's nothing but a ruse. He's retreated and left fires and noise behind to fool us."

"I doubt it," said Bagration. "I saw them on that hill this evening. If they'd retreated, they would have pulled out from there too... Officer!" he said to Rostov. "Are the enemy's skirmishers still in position?"
"They were there this evening, but I can't say for certain now, your excellency. Shall I ride out with some of my hussars to check?" Rostov replied.
Bagration stopped and tried to make out Rostov's face through the mist before answering.
"Well, go and see," he said after a pause.
"Yes, sir."

Rostov spurred his horse, called Sergeant Fedchenko and two other hussars, told them to follow, and trotted downhill toward the source of the shouting. He felt both scared and excited to be riding alone with three hussars into that mysterious, dangerous, misty unknown where no one had gone before him. Bagration called after him from the hilltop not to cross the stream, but Rostov pretended not to hear and kept riding on, continually mistaking bushes for trees and ditches for men, and continually realizing his mistakes. After descending the hill at a trot, he could no longer see either the Russian or the French campfires, but he heard the French shouting more loudly and clearly. In the valley ahead he saw what looked like a river, but when he reached it, he found it was a road. Coming out onto the road, he reined in his horse, hesitating whether to follow it or cross it and ride up the black hillside. Staying on the road, which gleamed white through the mist, would have been safer — easier to spot people coming. "Follow me!" he said. He crossed the road and began galloping uphill toward where the French pickets had been posted that evening.

"Your honor, there he is!" cried one of the hussars behind him. And before Rostov could make out what the dark shape in the fog was, there was a flash, a report, and a bullet whizzed high overhead through the mist with a mournful whine and passed out of hearing. Another musket misfired but flashed in the pan. Rostov wheeled his horse around and galloped back. Four more shots rang out at intervals, the bullets whistling past somewhere in the fog, each with a different pitch. Rostov eased his horse to a walk — the animal's spirits had risen with the firing, just like his own — and headed back at a leisurely pace. "More! Come on, more!" a happy voice said inside him. But no more shots came.
Only when he was close to Bagration did Rostov let his horse gallop again, and he rode up to the general with his hand at the salute.
Dolgorukov was still insisting that the French had retreated and had only left fires behind to trick them.
"What does that prove?" he was saying as Rostov rode up. "They could retreat and leave the pickets."
"It's clear they haven't all gone, Prince," said Bagration. "Let's wait until tomorrow morning — we'll find out everything then."

"The picket is still on the hill, your excellency — right where it was this evening," Rostov reported, leaning forward with his hand at the salute, unable to suppress the smile of exhilaration that his ride and especially the sound of the bullets had produced.
"Very good, very good," said Bagration. "Thank you, officer."
"Your excellency," said Rostov, "may I ask a favor?"
"What is it?"
"Our squadron is supposed to be in reserve tomorrow. May I request to be attached to the first squadron?"
"What's your name?"
"Count Rostov."
"Oh, very well — you may remain in my personal retinue."
"Count Ilya Rostov's son?" asked Dolgorukov.
But Rostov didn't reply.
"Then I can count on it, your excellency?"
"I'll give the order."
"Tomorrow I might even be sent with a message to the Emperor," Rostov thought.
"Thank God!"

The fires and shouting in the enemy camp were caused by the fact that Napoleon's proclamation was being read to the troops, and the Emperor himself was riding through his bivouacs. The soldiers, catching sight of him, lit bundles of straw and ran after him shouting, "Long live the Emperor!" Napoleon's proclamation read as follows:

Soldiers! The Russian army is advancing against you to avenge the Austrian army of Ulm. These are the same battalions you crushed at Hollabrunn and have been chasing ever since. The position we hold is a strong one, and while they march to outflank me on the right, they will expose their flank. Soldiers! I will personally direct your battalions. I will stay out of the firing line if, with your customary bravery, you carry chaos and confusion into the enemy's ranks. But should victory be in doubt even for a moment, you will see your Emperor expose himself to the enemy's first blows, for there must be no uncertainty about victory — especially on this day, when the honor of the French infantry is at stake, so vital to the honor of our nation.

Do not break ranks on the excuse of helping the wounded! Let every man be filled with the conviction that we must defeat these mercenaries of England, who harbor such hatred for our nation! This victory will end our campaign, and we can return to winter quarters where fresh French troops being raised in France will join us. The peace I will then make will be worthy of my people, of you, and of myself.
NAPOLEON

title: Book Three (1805) — Chapter 15
paragraphs: At eight o'clock, Kutuzov rode toward Pratzen at the head of the fourth column — Miloradovich's — which was supposed to replace the columns of Przhebyshevsky and Langeron, both of which had already descended into the valley. He greeted the soldiers of the lead regiment and gave the order to march, signaling that he intended to lead this column himself. When they reached the village of Pratzen, he halted. Prince Andrei rode behind, lost among the enormous crowd that made up the commander in chief's retinue. He was in a state of suppressed excitement and agitation, though outwardly calm — the way a person gets when a long-anticipated moment is finally at hand. He was firmly convinced that this would be his Toulon, his bridge of Arcole. He didn't know exactly how it would happen, but he was certain it would. He knew the terrain and the positions of the troops as well as anyone in the army could. His own strategic plan, now clearly impossible to carry out, had been set aside. Instead, working within Weyrother's plan, Prince Andrei considered possible developments and formed new projects that might call for his quick thinking and decisive action.

Down to the left, through the mist, the crackle of musket fire from unseen forces could be heard. That was where Prince Andrei expected the fighting to intensify. "That's where the difficulties will come," he thought, "and that's where I'll be sent with a brigade or a division. There, with the standard in my hand, I'll charge forward and break through whatever stands in my way."
He couldn't look calmly at the regimental standards as the battalions passed by. Each time he saw one, he kept thinking: "That might be the very standard I'll carry when I lead the army."

By morning, all that remained of the night's fog on the heights was a thin frost turning to dew, but down in the valleys it still lay like a sea of white milk. Nothing was visible in the valley to the left, where the troops had descended and where the gunfire was coming from. Above the heights stretched a dark, clear sky, and to the right hung the vast disk of the sun. In the distance, on the far shore of that misty sea, some wooded hills were just barely visible — the enemy was probably there, since something could be made out moving. To the right, the Guards were entering the mist with the sound of hooves and wheels, and now and then a glint of bayonets; to the left, beyond the village, similar masses of cavalry appeared and vanished into the white sea. In front and behind, infantry moved forward. The commander in chief stood at the edge of the village, watching the troops pass. That morning, Kutuzov seemed worn out and irritable. The infantry marching past him suddenly came to a halt without any order being given, apparently blocked by something ahead.

"Order them to form battalion columns and go around the village!" he said angrily to a general who had ridden up. "Don't you understand, your excellency, my dear sir, that you can't march through narrow village streets when we're advancing against the enemy?"
"I was planning to re-form them on the other side of the village, your excellency," the general replied.
Kutuzov gave a bitter laugh.
"That'll work out wonderfully — deploying in full view of the enemy! Just wonderful!"
"The enemy is still far away, your excellency. According to the battle plan —"
"The battle plan!" Kutuzov snapped bitterly. "Who told you that? Do as you're ordered."
"Yes, sir."
"My dear fellow," Nesvitsky whispered to Prince Andrei, "the old man is in a foul mood."
An Austrian officer in a white uniform with green plumes on his hat galloped up to Kutuzov and asked, on behalf of the Emperor, whether the fourth column had advanced into action.

Kutuzov turned away without answering, and his gaze happened to fall on Prince Andrei standing beside him. When he saw him, Kutuzov's bitter, caustic expression softened, as if acknowledging that none of this was his adjutant's fault. Still ignoring the Austrian, he addressed Bolkonsky.
"Go, my dear fellow, and see whether the third division has passed the village. Tell them to stop and wait for my orders."
Prince Andrei had barely started when Kutuzov stopped him.
"And find out if they've posted sharpshooters," he added. "What are they doing? What are they doing?" he muttered to himself, still not answering the Austrian.
Prince Andrei galloped off to carry out the order.

Riding past the advancing battalions, he stopped the third division and confirmed that there were indeed no sharpshooters deployed ahead of the columns. The colonel leading the regiment was shocked by the commander in chief's order to send out skirmishers. He had been certain there were other troops in front of him and that the enemy must be at least six miles away. In truth, nothing was visible ahead except a barren slope hidden by thick mist. After issuing orders in the commander in chief's name to correct this oversight, Prince Andrei galloped back. Kutuzov was still in the same place, his heavy body sagging wearily in the saddle, yawning with closed eyes. The troops had stopped and now stood with the butts of their muskets resting on the ground.
"All right, all right!" he said to Prince Andrei, then turned to a general who, watch in hand, was insisting it was time to move since all the left-flank columns had already gone down.
"Plenty of time, your excellency," Kutuzov muttered through a yawn. "Plenty of time," he repeated.

Just then, from somewhere behind Kutuzov, came the sound of regiments cheering, and the wave of salutes rolled rapidly closer along the whole extended line of advancing Russian columns. Clearly, whoever they were greeting was riding quickly. When the soldiers in the regiment nearest Kutuzov began to shout, he moved off to the side a little and looked back with a frown. A squadron-like group of horsemen in various uniforms came galloping along the road from Pratzen. Two of them rode ahead, side by side, at full gallop. One wore a black uniform with white plumes and rode a short-tailed chestnut horse; the other wore white and rode a black horse. These were the two Emperors, followed by their entourages. Kutuzov, putting on the manner of a grizzled old soldier at the front, called out "Attention!" and rode up to the Emperors with a salute. His entire appearance and demeanor were suddenly transformed. He adopted the air of a subordinate who obeys without question. With a show of deference that clearly struck Alexander as excessive, he rode up and saluted.

This unpleasant impression merely passed across the young and joyful face of the Emperor like a wisp of haze drifting over a clear sky, and was gone. After his illness, he looked somewhat thinner than he had on the field of Olmutz, where Bolkonsky had first seen him abroad. But there was still the same captivating blend of majesty and gentleness in his fine gray eyes, and on his delicate lips the same ability to shift expression, with the same prevailing look of warmhearted, innocent youth.

At the Olmutz review, he had seemed more majestic; here he seemed brighter and more full of energy. He was slightly flushed from galloping two miles, and as he reined in his horse, he sighed with relief and looked around at his companions — all of them as young and animated as himself. Czartoryski, Novosiltsev, Prince Volkonsky, Strogonov, and the rest — all richly dressed, cheerful young men on splendid, well-groomed, barely warm horses — had stopped behind the Emperor, exchanging remarks and smiling. Emperor Francis, a rosy, long-faced young man, sat very straight on his handsome black horse, looking about in a leisurely and preoccupied way. He beckoned to one of his white-uniformed adjutants and asked some question. "He's probably asking what time they set out," thought Prince Andrei, watching this old acquaintance with a smile he couldn't suppress as he recalled his reception at Brunn. Among the two Emperors' retinues were the finest young orderly officers from the Guard and line regiments, both Russian and Austrian. Mixed in among them were grooms leading the Tsar's beautiful reserve horses draped in embroidered cloths.
