The way a gust of fresh air from the fields sweeps into a stuffy room when a window is opened — that was how a rush of youthfulness, energy, and confidence reached Kutuzov's gloomy staff as all these brilliant young men came galloping up.
"Why haven't you started, Mikhail Ilarionovich?" Emperor Alexander asked Kutuzov quickly, at the same time casting a courteous glance at Emperor Francis.
"I'm waiting, Your Majesty," Kutuzov answered, bowing forward respectfully.
The Emperor frowned slightly and leaned his ear forward as if he hadn't quite heard.
"Waiting, Your Majesty," Kutuzov repeated. (Prince Andrei noticed that Kutuzov's upper lip twitched unnaturally as he said the word "waiting.") "Not all the columns have formed up yet, Your Majesty."
The Tsar heard but clearly didn't like the reply. He shrugged his somewhat rounded shoulders and glanced at Novosiltsev, who stood nearby, as if to complain about Kutuzov.

"You know, Mikhail Ilarionovich, we're not on the parade ground, where the review doesn't begin until all the troops are assembled," the Tsar said with another glance at Emperor Francis, as if inviting him — if not to join in — at least to listen. But Emperor Francis continued to look around and didn't seem to be listening.

"That is exactly why I have not begun, sire," Kutuzov said in a loud, clear voice, evidently making sure he would not go unheard, and again something in his face twitched. "That is exactly why I have not begun, sire — because we are not on parade and not on the Empress's Field." He spoke clearly and distinctly.
Everyone in the Emperor's retinue exchanged quick glances of displeasure and reproach. "Old as he may be, he shouldn't — he absolutely shouldn't — speak like that," their looks seemed to say.

The Tsar stared intently at Kutuzov's face, waiting for him to say something more. But Kutuzov, with his head respectfully bowed, appeared to be waiting as well. The silence stretched on for about a minute.
"However, if you command it, Your Majesty," Kutuzov said at last, raising his head and resuming his former tone — that of a dull, unquestioning, obedient general.
He nudged his horse forward and, calling over Miloradovich, the column commander, gave him the order to advance.
The troops began moving again, and two battalions of the Novgorod regiment and one of the Apsheron regiment marched past the Emperor.

As the Apsheron battalion went by, the red-faced Miloradovich — without his greatcoat, medals pinned to his chest, and a huge plume in his cocked hat worn sideways with corners pointing front and back — galloped energetically forward and reined in his horse before the Emperor with a dashing salute.
"God be with you, General!" said the Emperor.
"Ma foi, sire, nous ferons ce qui sera dans notre possibilité, sire," he answered cheerfully, though his poor French drew ironic smiles from the gentlemen in the Tsar's entourage.
* "Indeed, Sire, we shall do everything it is possible to do, Sire."

Miloradovich wheeled his horse sharply and positioned himself just behind the Emperor. The Apsheron soldiers, energized by the Tsar's presence, marched past the Emperors and their suites at a bold, brisk pace, keeping perfect step.

"Lads!" Miloradovich shouted in a loud, confident, and cheerful voice — so carried away by the sound of gunfire, the prospect of battle, and the sight of the gallant Apsherons (his old comrades from Suvorov's campaigns, now marching so splendidly past the Emperors) that he forgot the sovereigns were right there. "Lads, it's not the first village you've had to take!" he cried.
"Glad to do our best!" the soldiers shouted back.

The Emperor's horse startled at the sudden cry. This was the same horse that had carried the sovereign through reviews in Russia, and it carried him here too on the field of Austerlitz, bearing the absent-minded kicks of his left foot and pricking its ears at the sound of gunfire — just as it had done on the Empress's Field — without understanding the meaning of the shots, or the proximity of Emperor Francis's black horse, or anything that was being said, thought, and felt by its rider that day.
The Emperor turned with a smile to one of his attendants and said something, pointing at the brave Apsherons.

title: Book Three (1805) — Chapter 16
paragraphs: Kutuzov, accompanied by his adjutants, rode at a walk behind the carabiniers.

After less than half a mile, he stopped at an isolated, abandoned building that had probably once been a roadside inn, at a fork where two roads diverged. Both roads led downhill, and troops were marching along each of them.

The fog had started to thin, and enemy forces were dimly visible about a mile and a half away on the opposite heights. Down to the left, the firing grew more distinct. Kutuzov had stopped and was speaking with an Austrian general. Prince Andrei, riding a little behind, turned to an adjutant and asked to borrow a field glass.
"Look, look!" the adjutant said, staring not at the distant troops but down the hill in front of them. "It's the French!"

The two generals and the adjutant all grabbed at the field glass, trying to snatch it from one another. The look on every face suddenly turned to horror. The French were supposed to be a mile and a half away, but had appeared just in front of them — suddenly and without warning.
"Is that the enemy? No! Yes, look — it is! For certain. But how can that be?" different voices said.
With his naked eye, Prince Andrei could see below them, to the right, not more than five hundred paces from where Kutuzov stood, a dense French column advancing toward the Apsheron regiment.
"This is it! The decisive moment has come. My turn has arrived," Prince Andrei thought, and spurring his horse, he rode up to Kutuzov.

"The Apsherons must be stopped, your excellency!" he shouted. But at that very instant a cloud of smoke billowed in every direction, gunfire erupted at close range, and a voice of raw, terrified panic — barely two steps from Prince Andrei — screamed: "Brothers! We're done for!" And at that, as if on command, everyone began to run.

Confused and swelling crowds were streaming back toward the place where, just five minutes earlier, the troops had marched past the Emperors. It would have been impossible to stop that tide — you couldn't even avoid being swept along with it. Bolkonsky could only try not to lose touch with the retreating mass as he looked around in bewilderment, unable to grasp what was happening ahead. Nesvitsky, red-faced and angry, looking nothing like himself, was shouting at Kutuzov that he would certainly be taken prisoner if he didn't ride away immediately. Kutuzov stayed where he was. Without answering, he pulled out a handkerchief. Blood was flowing from his cheek. Prince Andrei forced his way to him.
"You're wounded?" he asked, barely managing to control the trembling of his jaw.

"The wound isn't here — it's there!" Kutuzov said, pressing the handkerchief to his wounded cheek and pointing at the fleeing soldiers. "Stop them!" he shouted, and at almost the same moment — probably realizing that stopping them was impossible — he spurred his horse and rode to the right.
A fresh wave of the fleeing mob caught him and carried him along with it.

The troops were running in such a dense mass that once you were caught among them, it was nearly impossible to get free. One man was shouting, "Move! Why are you blocking us?" Another, in the same spot, spun around and fired into the air. A third was hitting the horse Kutuzov himself was riding. With great difficulty, Kutuzov managed to break away to the left of the stampede. His suite was now reduced by more than half. They rode toward the sound of nearby artillery fire. Having also fought his way out of the flood of fugitives, Prince Andrei tried to keep close to Kutuzov. Through the smoke on the hillside, he could see a Russian battery still firing, with French soldiers running toward it. Higher up stood Russian infantry that was neither advancing to protect the battery nor retreating with the fleeing crowd. A mounted general broke away from the infantry and rode up to Kutuzov. Of his original suite, only four men remained. They were all pale, exchanging silent looks.

"Stop those cowards!" Kutuzov gasped to the regimental commander, pointing at the fleeing soldiers. But at that very instant — as if to punish him for those words — bullets came whistling across the regiment and across Kutuzov's group like a flock of small birds.

The French had attacked the battery and, spotting Kutuzov, were now shooting at him. After this volley, the regimental commander grabbed his leg; several soldiers dropped; and a second lieutenant holding the flag let it slip from his hands. It swayed and fell, but caught on the muskets of the nearest soldiers. The men began firing on their own, without orders.

"Oh! Oh! Oh!" Kutuzov groaned in despair, looking around. "Bolkonsky!" he whispered, his voice trembling with the frailty of age. "Bolkonsky!" he whispered again, pointing at the shattered battalion and at the enemy. "What is that?"
But before he had finished speaking, Prince Andrei — tears of shame and fury choking him — had already leapt from his horse and was running toward the standard.
"Forward, lads!" he shouted in a piercing, almost childlike voice.
"This is it!" he thought, grabbing the staff of the standard, and he heard with pleasure the whistle of bullets that were clearly aimed at him. Several soldiers fell around him.
"Hurrah!" Prince Andrei shouted, and barely able to hold up the heavy standard, he ran forward, fully confident that the entire battalion would follow him.

And indeed, he ran only a few steps alone. First one soldier moved, then another, and soon the whole battalion charged forward with a shout of "Hurrah!" and overtook him. A sergeant ran up and grabbed the flag, which was swaying from its weight in Prince Andrei's hands, but he was killed immediately. Prince Andrei seized the standard again and, dragging it by the staff, ran on with the battalion. Ahead he could see Russian artillerymen — some still fighting, others abandoning their guns and running toward him. He could also see French infantry soldiers seizing the artillery horses and turning the cannons around. Prince Andrei and the battalion were now within twenty paces of the guns. He heard the ceaseless whistle of bullets above him, and to his right and left soldiers kept groaning and falling. But he didn't look at them — he looked only at what was happening in front of him, at the battery. He could now clearly see a red-haired gunner with his cap knocked crooked, pulling one end of a ramrod while a French soldier tugged at the other. He could distinctly see the frantic yet angry expressions on both men's faces — they clearly had no idea what they were doing.

"What are they even doing?" Prince Andrei wondered, watching them. "Why doesn't the red-haired gunner run? He's unarmed. Why doesn't the Frenchman stab him? The gunner won't get away before the Frenchman remembers his bayonet and runs him through."

And sure enough, another French soldier came running up with his musket trailing behind him, heading straight for the two struggling men. The fate of the red-haired gunner — who had triumphantly secured the ramrod and still had no idea what was about to happen to him — was about to be decided. But Prince Andrei never saw how it ended. It felt as though one of the soldiers near him struck him on the head with the full swing of a club. It hurt, but what was worse was that the pain broke his concentration and kept him from seeing what he had been watching.

"What's this? Am I falling? My legs are giving way," he thought — and fell onto his back. He opened his eyes, hoping to see how the fight between the Frenchmen and the gunners had ended, whether the red-haired gunner had been killed, whether the cannon had been captured or saved. But he saw nothing. Above him now there was only the sky — the vast sky, not clear, yet immeasurably high, with gray clouds drifting slowly across it. "How quiet, how peaceful, how solemn — nothing like the way I was running," Prince Andrei thought. "Not the way we ran, shouting and fighting — not like the gunner and the Frenchman clawing at the ramrod with their frightened, angry faces. The clouds moving across that endless sky — how completely different they are from all of that. How is it I never noticed this sky before? And how happy I am to have found it at last! Yes! Everything is empty, everything is a lie — except this infinite sky. Nothing exists, nothing at all, except this. But even the sky doesn't really exist — there is nothing but stillness and peace. Thank God!"

title: Book Three (1805) — Chapter 17
paragraphs: On the right flank, commanded by Bagration, the battle had not yet begun at nine o'clock. Not wanting to agree to Dolgorukov's demand that he launch the attack, and hoping to avoid responsibility, Prince Bagration proposed sending a messenger to the commander in chief for instructions. Bagration knew perfectly well that since the distance between the two flanks was over six miles, even if the messenger wasn't killed along the way (which was very likely), and even if he managed to find the commander in chief (which would be extremely difficult), he still wouldn't make it back before evening.

Bagration let his large, expressionless, sleepy eyes wander across his staff, and the first face to catch his attention was the boyish face of Rostov, breathless with excitement and hope. He sent him.
"And if I meet His Majesty before I meet the commander in chief, your excellency?" Rostov asked, raising his hand to his cap.
"You may deliver the message to His Majesty," Dolgorukov cut in quickly, before Bagration could reply.

Having been relieved from picket duty, Rostov had managed to grab a few hours of sleep before dawn. He felt cheerful, bold, and full of purpose — his movements springy, his faith in his luck unshaken, and his overall state of mind one in which everything seems possible, pleasant, and easy.

Every one of his wishes was coming true that morning: a major battle was underway and he was part of it; better still, he was serving as orderly to the bravest general; and on top of that, he was riding off with a message for Kutuzov, and perhaps even for the sovereign himself. It was a bright morning, he had a strong horse under him, and his heart was full of joy and happiness. As soon as he received the order, he gave his horse its head and galloped along the line. At first he rode along Bagration's troops, which hadn't yet joined the fighting and stood motionless. Then he passed through the area held by Uvarov's cavalry, where he noticed preparations and a stir of activity. Beyond Uvarov's cavalry, he could clearly hear the sound of cannon and musket fire ahead of him. The firing grew louder.

In the fresh morning air, what he heard now was no longer the scattered musket shots at irregular intervals from before, followed by an occasional cannon blast. Instead, there was a continuous roll of musketry volleys from the slopes below Pratzen, broken by cannon reports so frequent that sometimes several of them merged together into a single roar.

He could see puffs of musketry smoke chasing each other down the hillsides, and clouds of cannon smoke rolling outward, spreading, and blending together. Through the smoke, he could also make out — by the glint of bayonets — moving masses of infantry and narrow lines of artillery with green ammunition wagons.

Rostov stopped his horse on a small hill to try to understand what was going on, but no matter how hard he strained his attention, he couldn't figure out or make sense of any of it. Down there in the smoke, men of some kind were moving around; lines of troops moved in the front and behind. But why, in which direction, and who they were — it was impossible to tell. Far from depressing or frightening him, the sights and sounds only heightened his energy and determination.
"Go on! Go on! Give it to them!" he cheered mentally at the sounds, and then continued galloping along the line, riding deeper and deeper into the area where the army was already engaged.
"What will happen there, I don't know, but it'll all work out!" Rostov thought.
After passing some Austrian troops, he noticed that the next section of the line — the Guards — was already in action.
"Even better! I'll get to see it up close," he thought.

He was riding almost along the front line. A cluster of men came galloping toward him — Uhlans, returning from an attack with their ranks in disarray. Rostov moved out of their way, involuntarily noticing that one of them was bleeding, and galloped on.

"That's not my concern," he thought. He hadn't gone many hundred yards when, off to his left, spanning the full width of the field, he saw an enormous body of cavalry in brilliant white uniforms mounted on black horses, trotting straight toward him and directly across his path. Rostov pushed his horse to full gallop to get clear of them, and he might have succeeded had they maintained their speed — but they kept going faster, and some of the horses were already at a full gallop. Rostov heard the pounding of hooves and the jingling of weapons, and he could see their horses, their figures, even their faces more and more clearly. These were the Horse Guards, advancing to attack the French cavalry that was riding to meet them.

The Horse Guards were galloping but still holding their horses in check. Rostov could already make out their faces and heard the command: "Charge!" shouted by an officer who was driving his thoroughbred to top speed. Fearing he would be crushed or dragged into the attack against the French, Rostov galloped along the front as fast as his horse could go, but still couldn't avoid them in time.

The last of the Horse Guards — a massive, pockmarked fellow — scowled angrily at seeing Rostov in his path, knowing a collision was inevitable. This Guardsman would certainly have knocked Rostov and his Bedouin horse flat (Rostov felt positively tiny and weak next to these enormous men and their horses), had Rostov not thought to crack his whip in front of the Guardsman's horse. The big black horse, sixteen hands high, shied and pinned back its ears. But the pockmarked Guardsman dug in his huge spurs, and the horse flicked its tail, stretched out its neck, and charged forward even faster. The Horse Guards had barely passed Rostov when he heard them shout "Hurrah!" and, looking back, he saw their front ranks tangled up with foreign cavalry wearing red shoulder pieces — probably French. He could see nothing more after that, because suddenly cannon began firing from somewhere and smoke covered everything.

At that moment, as the Horse Guards disappeared into the smoke beyond him, Rostov hesitated: should he gallop after them, or continue on to where he'd been sent? This was the brilliant charge of the Horse Guards that stunned even the French. Rostov was horrified to learn later that out of that entire mass of huge, handsome men — all those brilliant, wealthy young officers and cadets who had galloped past him on their thousand-ruble horses — only eighteen survived the charge.
"Why should I envy them? My chance hasn't passed, and maybe I'll see the Emperor any minute now!" Rostov thought, and galloped on.

When he came level with the Foot Guards, he became aware that cannonballs were flying nearby — not so much from hearing them as from seeing the anxious looks on the soldiers' faces and the forced, unnatural solemnity of the officers.
As he passed behind one of the Foot Guard regiment's lines, a voice called out his name.
"Rostov!"
"What?" he answered, not recognizing Boris.
"Guess what — we were in the front line! Our regiment attacked!" Boris said with the bright, happy smile of a young man who has been under fire for the first time.
Rostov stopped.
"Really? How did it go?"

"We drove them back!" Boris said excitedly, becoming talkative. "Can you imagine it?" And he launched into a story about how the Guards had taken up their position and spotted troops ahead, assumed they were Austrians, and then suddenly realized from the cannonballs raining down on them that they were actually on the front line and had to go into action unexpectedly. Rostov spurred his horse before Boris had finished.
"Where are you headed?" Boris asked.
"To deliver a message to His Majesty."

"There he is!" Boris said, thinking Rostov had said "His Highness," and pointing to the Grand Duke, who stood a hundred paces away in his helmet and Horse Guards jacket, his high shoulders squared and brows knitted, shouting something at a pale, white-uniformed Austrian officer.
"But that's the Grand Duke — I need the commander in chief, or the Emperor," Rostov said, about to spur his horse forward.

"Count! Count!" Berg shouted, running up from the other side, just as eager as Boris. "Count! I've been wounded in my right hand" — and he showed his bleeding hand wrapped in a handkerchief — "and I stayed at the front! I held my sword in my left hand, Count. Our whole family — the von Bergs — have always been knights!"
He said something more, but Rostov didn't wait to hear it and rode away.

Having passed the Guards and crossed an open stretch, Rostov — wanting to avoid being caught in front of the first line again, as he had been during the Horse Guards' charge — followed the line of reserves, giving a wide berth to the areas with the heaviest musket and cannon fire. Suddenly he heard musket fire very close, directly in front of him and behind the Russian positions — somewhere the enemy should not have been.

"What's going on?" he thought. "The enemy behind our army? That's impossible!" And suddenly he was seized by a wave of fear — fear for himself and for the outcome of the whole battle. "But whatever happens," he told himself, "there's no way around it now. I have to find the commander in chief right here, and if everything is lost, then I'll die with the rest."
The sense of dread that had suddenly gripped Rostov only grew stronger the farther he rode into the area behind the village of Pratzen, which was teeming with troops of every kind.
"What does it mean? What's happening? Who are they firing at? Who's doing the firing?" Rostov kept asking as he encountered Russian and Austrian soldiers running in confused crowds across his path.
"The devil only knows! Everyone's been killed! It's all over!" he was told in Russian, German, and Czech by the fleeing crowds, who understood what was happening no better than he did.
"Kill the Germans!" one man shouted.
"To hell with them — the traitors!"
"Zum Henker diese Russen!" muttered a German.
* "Hang these Russians!"

Several wounded men came along the road, and curses, screams, and groans all merged into a general uproar. Then the firing died away. Rostov later learned that Russian and Austrian soldiers had been shooting at each other.

"My God! What does this all mean?" he thought. "And right here, where the Emperor himself might see it any moment. But no — these must just be a handful of rotten soldiers. It'll be over soon. It can't really be as bad as it looks — it just can't! If I can just get past them — quickly, quickly!"

The very idea of defeat and flight could not enter Rostov's mind. Even though he saw French cannon and French troops on the Pratzen Heights — the very place where he'd been sent to look for the commander in chief — he could not, and would not, believe it.

title: Book Three (1805) — Chapter 18
paragraphs: Rostov had been sent to find Kutuzov and the Emperor near the village of Pratzen. But neither they nor any commanding officer was there — only disorganized mobs of troops of every kind. He pushed his already exhausted horse forward, trying to get through the crowds as quickly as possible, but the farther he went, the worse the chaos became. The main road was clogged with carriages and vehicles of every description, and with Russian and Austrian soldiers — some wounded, some not. This whole mass surged and jostled in confusion under the grim accompaniment of cannonballs flying from the French batteries on the Pratzen Heights.
"Where is the Emperor? Where is Kutuzov?" Rostov kept asking everyone he could stop, but no one could give him an answer.
Finally, he grabbed a soldier by the collar and forced him to respond.
"Come on, brother! They all cleared out ages ago!" the soldier said with a laugh for some reason, shaking himself free.

Leaving that soldier, who was clearly drunk, Rostov stopped the horse of an orderly or groom belonging to some important personage and began questioning him. The man said the Tsar had been driven past in a carriage at top speed about an hour ago on this very road, and that he was dangerously wounded.
"That can't be true!" Rostov said. "It must have been someone else."

"I saw him with my own eyes," the man replied with the self-assured, slightly mocking smile of someone who knows what he's talking about. "By now I'd think I know what the Emperor looks like, after all the times I've seen him in Petersburg. I saw him just as clearly as I see you. There he sat in the carriage, white as a sheet. The way they drove those four black horses — my God, they flew! I think by now I know the imperial horses, and I know Ilya Ivanich. I don't think Ilya drives anyone but the Tsar!"
Rostov let go of the horse and was about to ride on when a wounded officer passing by spoke to him.
"Who are you looking for?" the officer asked. "The commander in chief? He was killed by a cannonball — hit right in the chest, in front of our regiment."
"Not killed — wounded!" another officer corrected him.
"Who? Kutuzov?" Rostov asked.

"Not Kutuzov, but what's-his-name — well, never mind. There aren't many left alive. Head that way, to the village over there. All the commanders are gathered there," the officer said, pointing toward the village of Hosjeradek, and walked on.

Rostov rode on at a slow pace, no longer knowing why or where he was going. The Emperor was wounded, the battle lost. It was impossible to doubt it now. Rostov rode in the direction he'd been pointed, toward a village where he could see steeples and a church. What was the rush? What was he supposed to say to the Tsar or to Kutuzov now, even if they were alive and unhurt?
"Take that road, your honor — go the other way or you'll be killed on the spot!" a soldier shouted to him. "They'll kill you over there!"
"Oh, what are you talking about?" said another. "Where's he supposed to go? That way's shorter."
Rostov thought it over, then went in the direction where they said he'd be killed.

"What difference does it make now? If the Emperor is wounded, why should I try to save myself?" he thought. He rode into the area where the greatest number of men had died fleeing from Pratzen. The French hadn't yet occupied this ground, and the Russians — those who were uninjured or only slightly wounded — had abandoned it long ago. Scattered across the field, like heaps of manure on well-tended farmland, lay clusters of ten to fifteen dead and wounded for every two acres. The wounded had crawled together in groups of two and three, and their agonized screams and groans could be heard — some of which sounded exaggerated, or so it seemed to Rostov. He urged his horse into a trot to avoid looking at these suffering men. He was afraid — but not for his life. He was afraid that his courage, which he knew he needed, would not survive the sight of these unfortunates.

The French, who had stopped firing at this field strewn with dead and wounded — since there was no one left to shoot at — spotted a lone adjutant riding across it, aimed a cannon at him, and fired several shots. The terrifying whistle of the shells and the sight of the corpses all around merged in Rostov's mind into a single overwhelming feeling of horror and self-pity. He thought of his mother's last letter. "What would she feel," he wondered, "if she could see me right now, on this field, with the cannon aimed at me?"

In the village of Hosjeradek, Russian troops were pulling back from the battlefield. Although still somewhat disorganized, they were in less confusion here. The French cannon couldn't reach this far, and the musket fire sounded distant. Here, everyone could clearly see — and openly said — that the battle was lost. No one Rostov asked could tell him where the Emperor or Kutuzov was. Some confirmed that the Emperor had been wounded; others said he hadn't, and explained the false rumor by the fact that the Emperor's carriage had indeed gone racing off the battlefield carrying the pale, terrified chief court marshal, Count Tolstoy, who had ridden out to the field with others in the Emperor's retinue. One officer told Rostov he'd seen someone from headquarters behind the village, off to the left. Rostov rode that way — not expecting to find anyone, but simply to ease his conscience. After riding about two miles and passing the last of the Russian troops, he spotted two men on horseback near a kitchen garden surrounded by a ditch. One of them, wearing a white plume in his hat, looked familiar. The other, mounted on a beautiful chestnut horse (which Rostov thought he'd seen before), rode up to the ditch, dug in his spurs, and leapt lightly over it. Only a little dirt crumbled from the bank under the horse's hind hooves. He turned the horse sharply, jumped back over the ditch, and respectfully addressed the rider with the white plumes, apparently suggesting he do the same. The rider — whose figure seemed familiar to Rostov and held his gaze — made a gesture of refusal with his head and hand, and by that gesture Rostov instantly recognized his beloved, adored sovereign.

"But it can't be him — alone, in the middle of this empty field!" Rostov thought. Just then, Alexander turned his head, and Rostov saw the beloved features that were etched so deeply into his memory. The Emperor was pale, his cheeks sunken, his eyes hollow — but the charm and gentleness of his face were all the more striking for it. Rostov was overjoyed to confirm that the rumors of the Emperor being wounded were false. He was happy just to be seeing him. He knew that he could — and even should — ride straight up and deliver the message Dolgorukov had ordered him to carry.

But just as a young man in love trembles, loses his nerve, and can't bring himself to say the words he's rehearsed through sleepless nights — looking instead for an excuse to delay or flee when the longed-for moment finally arrives and he finds himself alone with her — so Rostov, now that he had achieved what he wanted more than anything in the world, had no idea how to approach the Emperor. A thousand reasons occurred to him why it would be awkward, inappropriate, and impossible.

"What am I thinking? It's as though I'm glad to find him alone and upset! A stranger's face might be unwelcome, even painful to him in this moment of sorrow. And besides, what could I possibly say to him when my heart is failing me and my mouth goes dry just looking at him?" Not a single one of the countless speeches he'd composed in his imagination — all those speeches addressed to the Emperor — could he recall now. Those speeches had been meant for entirely different circumstances; most of them were to be delivered in moments of victory and glory, usually as he lay dying from his wounds and the sovereign thanked him for his heroic deeds, and with his dying breath he declared the love his actions had proved.

"And how can I ask the Emperor for orders for the right flank when it's nearly four o'clock and the battle is already lost? No — I absolutely must not approach him. I must not intrude on his thoughts. Better to die a thousand deaths than to risk a cold look or a harsh word from him," Rostov decided. Filled with sorrow and a heart full of despair, he rode away, glancing back constantly at the Tsar, who remained standing in the same pose of indecision.

While Rostov was arguing with himself and riding sadly away, Captain von Toll happened to ride to the same spot. Seeing the Emperor, he immediately rode up, offered his assistance, and helped him cross the ditch on foot. The Emperor, wanting to rest and feeling unwell, sat down beneath an apple tree, and von Toll stayed at his side. From a distance, Rostov watched with envy and regret as von Toll spoke at length and with feeling to the Emperor, and the Emperor — clearly weeping — covered his eyes with his hand and pressed von Toll's.
"That could have been me!" Rostov thought, and barely holding back tears of pity for the Emperor, he rode on in complete despair, no longer knowing where he was going or why.
His despair was made all the worse by the knowledge that his own weakness was the cause of his grief.

He could have — not just could have, but should have — gone up to the sovereign. It had been a once-in-a-lifetime chance to prove his devotion to the Emperor, and he had let it slip away. "What have I done?" he thought. He turned his horse around and galloped back to the place where he'd seen the Emperor, but there was no one there now. Only carts and carriages were rolling by. From one of the drivers, he learned that Kutuzov's staff was nearby, in the village the vehicles were headed for. Rostov followed them. Ahead of him walked Kutuzov's groom, leading horses draped in blankets. Then came a cart, and behind it walked an old, bowlegged house servant in a pointed cap and sheepskin coat.
"Tit! Hey, Tit!" said the groom.
"What?" the old man answered absently.
"Go on, Tit! Do some threshing!"
"Oh, you fool!" the old man said, spitting in annoyance. A little time passed in silence, and then the same joke was repeated.
By five in the evening, the battle had been lost on every front. More than a hundred cannons were already in French hands.
Przhebyshevsky and his entire corps had surrendered. Other columns, having lost half their men, were retreating in disorderly, chaotic masses.
The remnants of Langeron's and Dokhturov's combined forces were crowding around the dams and banks of the ponds near the village of Augesd.

After five o'clock, the only fighting still to be heard was a fierce cannonade — from French guns alone — fired from batteries lined up along the slopes of the Pratzen Heights at the retreating Russian forces.

In the rearguard, Dokhturov and others had rallied several battalions and were keeping up a musketry fire against the French cavalry pursuing the Russian troops. Dusk was falling. On the narrow Augesd Dam — where for so many years the old miller had sat in his tasseled cap, peacefully fishing while his grandson, sleeves rolled up, handled the slippery, silvery fish in the watering can; on that same dam where for years Moravians in shaggy caps and blue jackets had peacefully driven their two-horse carts loaded with wheat and returned dusty with flour — on that narrow dam, among the wagons and the cannons, under the horses' hooves and between the wagon wheels, men disfigured by the terror of death now crushed together, trampling one another, dying, stepping over the dying, and killing each other — all just to advance a few steps before being killed in exactly the same way.
Every ten seconds, a cannonball came screaming through the air, or a shell exploded in the middle of the dense crowd, killing some and spattering those nearby with blood.

Dolokhov — now an officer — was wounded in the arm and on foot, along with the regimental commander on horseback and about ten men from his company. They were all that remained of the entire regiment. Swept forward by the crowd, they had gotten jammed at the approach to the dam and stood packed together on all sides because a horse ahead had collapsed under a cannon and the crowd was struggling to drag it free. A cannonball killed someone behind them; another landed in front and splattered Dolokhov with blood. The crowd, pushing forward in desperation, squeezed together, moved a few steps, and stopped again.
"Get a hundred yards farther and we're saved for sure; stay here two more minutes and it's certain death," each man thought.
Dolokhov, caught in the middle of the crowd, shoved his way to the edge of the dam, knocking two soldiers off their feet, and ran out onto the slippery ice covering the millpond.
"This way!" he shouted, jumping on the ice, which cracked beneath him. "This way!" he yelled to the men with the cannon. "It holds!"

The ice held him, but it sagged and groaned, and it was obvious that it would give way — not only under a cannon or a crowd, but very soon even under his weight alone. The men watched him and edged toward the bank, but hesitated to step onto the ice. The general on horseback at the entrance to the dam raised his hand and opened his mouth to say something to Dolokhov. Suddenly a cannonball came shrieking so low over the crowd that everyone ducked. It smacked into something wet, and the general fell from his horse into a pool of blood. No one gave him a second look or thought of picking him up.

"Get on the ice! Over the ice! Move! Turn! Don't you hear? Move!" countless voices began shouting all at once after the cannonball struck the general — the men not even knowing what they were shouting or why.

One of the trailing cannons heading for the dam veered off onto the ice. Crowds of soldiers from the dam began running onto the frozen pond. The ice broke under one of the first soldiers, and his leg plunged into the water. He tried to right himself but fell in up to his waist. The nearest soldiers pulled back; the gun driver stopped his horse. But from behind came more shouts: "Onto the ice! Why are you stopping? Go on! Go on!" And screams of terror rose from the crowd. The soldiers near the cannon waved their arms and beat the horses to get them moving. The horses stepped off the bank. The ice, which had held under the men on foot, collapsed in a great slab, and some forty men who were standing on it plunged in — some lurching forward, some backward — drowning each other.
Still the cannonballs kept whistling and thudding steadily onto the ice and into the water, and most often of all into the mass of humanity covering the dam, the pond, and the bank.

title: Book Four (1806) — Chapter 2
paragraphs: After returning to Moscow from the army, Nicholas Rostov was welcomed by his household as the best of sons, a hero, and their darling Nikolenka; by his relatives as a charming, attractive, and well-mannered young man; and by his acquaintances as a handsome hussar lieutenant, a good dancer, and one of the best catches in the city.

The Rostovs knew everyone in Moscow. The old count had enough money that year, since all his estates had been remortgaged, so Nicholas — having acquired his own racing horse, the most fashionable riding breeches (a style no one else in Moscow had yet), and the latest boots with sharply pointed toes and small silver spurs — had a very good time. After a short period of readjusting to civilian life, Nicholas found it quite pleasant to be home again. He felt that he had grown up and matured considerably. His old despair over failing a Scripture exam, borrowing money from Gavril to pay a sleigh driver, secretly kissing Sonya — he now looked back on all of it as childishness he had left far behind. Now he was a lieutenant of hussars in a silver-braided jacket, wearing the Cross of St. George — a medal awarded for bravery in combat — and he was training a racing horse with well-known, older, respected horsemen. He had a lady acquaintance on one of the boulevards whom he visited in the evenings. He led the mazurka at the Arkharovs' ball, discussed the war with Field Marshal Kamenski, frequented the English Club, and was on friendly terms with a forty-year-old colonel to whom Denisov had introduced him.

His passion for the Emperor had cooled somewhat in Moscow. Still, since he didn't see him and had no opportunity to, he often spoke about him and about his devotion, hinting that he hadn't told everything — that there was something in his feelings for the Emperor that not everyone could understand. With his whole heart he shared the adoration then common in Moscow for the Emperor, who was referred to as "the angel incarnate."

During Rostov's short stay in Moscow before returning to the army, he didn't grow closer to Sonya — if anything, he drifted away from her. She was very pretty and sweet, and clearly deeply in love with him, but he was at that age when there seems to be so much to do that there's no time for love, and a young man values his freedom, which he needs for so many other things. When he thought of Sonya, he told himself, "There will be plenty of girls like her — girls I haven't even met yet. There'll be time enough to think about love when I want to, but right now I have no time." Besides, the company of women struck him as somehow beneath his manhood. He went to balls and into ladies' society while making a show of doing it reluctantly. The races, the English Club, drinking bouts with Denisov, and visits to a certain house — that was a different matter entirely, and perfectly fitting for a dashing young hussar!
At the beginning of March, old Count Ilya Rostov was consumed with arranging a dinner in honor of Prince Bagration at the English Club.

The count paced the hall in his dressing gown, issuing orders to the club steward and to the famous Feoktist, the club's head chef, about asparagus, fresh cucumbers, strawberries, veal, and fish for the dinner. The count had been a founding member and committee member of the club. They had entrusted him with organizing the Bagration celebration because few people knew how to put on a lavish, generous feast like he did, and fewer still would be as willing and able to cover shortfalls from their own pocket. The chef and steward listened to his orders with pleased expressions, knowing that under no other management could they so easily skim a handsome profit from a dinner costing several thousand rubles.
"Now remember — cocks' combs in the turtle soup, you hear!"
"Three cold dishes, then?" asked the chef.
The count considered.
"Can't have fewer — yes, three... The mayonnaise, that's one," he said, counting on his fingers.
"Should I order those large sterlets?" asked the steward.

"Yes, we'll have to — they won't sell them for less. Oh dear, I almost forgot — we need another side dish. Good heavens!" he clutched his head. "Who's going to get me the flowers? Dmitri! Hey, Dmitri! Run out to our Moscow estate," he said to the factotum who appeared at his call. "Hurry up and tell Maksim the gardener to put the servants to work. Everything from the hothouses must be brought here, wrapped carefully in felt. I need two hundred pots here by Friday."

After giving several more orders, he was about to go see his "little countess" for a rest when he remembered something else important. He came back, called the chef and steward again, and resumed giving directions. Light footsteps and the clink of spurs sounded at the door, and the young count walked in — handsome, rosy-cheeked, with a dark little mustache, visibly rested and looking sleeker from his comfortable Moscow life.

"Ah, my boy, my head's spinning!" said the old man with a smile, looking slightly embarrassed in front of his son. "If only you'd help a little! I need singers too. I'll have my own orchestra, but should we also bring in the gypsy singers? You military types like that sort of thing."
"Really, Papa, I think Prince Bagration worried less before the Battle of Schon Grabern than you're worrying now," said his son with a smile.
The old count pretended to be offended.
"Easy for you to say — try doing it yourself!"
And the count turned to the chef, who watched the father and son with a shrewd, respectful, and sympathetic expression.
"What are young people coming to these days, eh, Feoktist?" he said. "Laughing at us old fellows!"
"That's right, your excellency. All they have to do is eat a good dinner — but putting it all together and serving it, that's not their department!"

"Exactly!" exclaimed the count, and cheerfully seizing his son by both hands, he cried, "Now I've got you! Take the sleigh and pair right away and go to Bezukhov's. Tell him Count Ilya sent you to ask for strawberries and fresh pineapples. We can't get them from anyone else. He's not there himself, so you'll have to go in and ask the princesses. And from there, head to Razgulyay — the coachman Ipatka knows the way — and find the gypsy Ilyushka, the one who danced at Count Orlov's in a white Cossack coat, and bring him to me."
"And should I bring the gypsy girls along too?" asked Nicholas, laughing. "Oh, dear..."

At that moment, with quiet footsteps and the businesslike, preoccupied, yet meekly pious expression that never left her face, Anna Mikhaylovna entered the hall. Though she found the count in his dressing gown every day, he always became flustered and apologized for his appearance.

"Not at all, my dear count," she said, modestly lowering her eyes. "But I'll go to Bezukhov's myself. Pierre has arrived, and now we can get whatever we need from his hothouses. I need to see him anyway. He's forwarded me a letter from Boris. Thank God, Boris is now on the staff."
The count was delighted that Anna Mikhaylovna was taking one of his errands off his hands, and he ordered the small closed carriage for her.
"Tell Bezukhov to come. I'll put his name on the list. Is his wife with him?" he asked.
Anna Mikhaylovna raised her eyes to the ceiling, and an expression of deep sorrow crossed her face.

"Oh, my dear friend, his situation is very unfortunate," she said. "If what we hear is true, it's terrible. How little we imagined such a thing when we were celebrating his happiness! And such a pure, angelic soul as young Bezukhov! Yes, I feel for him deeply and will try to offer what comfort I can."
"What — what's happened?" asked both the young and old Rostov.
Anna Mikhaylovna sighed deeply.

"Dolokhov — Maria Ivanovna's son," she said in a conspiratorial whisper, "has completely compromised her, they say. Pierre took him in, invited him to stay at his house in Petersburg, and now... she's come here, and that daredevil followed her!" said Anna Mikhaylovna, intending to show sympathy for Pierre, but betraying through her tone and a half-smile that her sympathies lay partly with the "daredevil," as she called Dolokhov. "They say Pierre is absolutely devastated."
"Dear, dear! Still, tell him to come to the club — it'll all blow over. It's going to be an incredible banquet."

The next day, March third, shortly after one o'clock, two hundred and fifty members of the English Club and fifty guests were waiting for the guest of honor and hero of the Austrian campaign, Prince Bagration, to arrive for dinner.

When news of the Battle of Austerlitz first reached Moscow, the city had been stunned. Russians were so accustomed to victories that when they heard of the defeat, some simply refused to believe it, while others searched for some extraordinary explanation. At the English Club — where everyone distinguished, important, and well-informed gathered — when the news began arriving in December, no one spoke about the war or the battle, as though everyone had agreed to stay silent. The men who set the tone in conversation — Count Rostopchin, Prince Yuri Dolgorukov, Valuev, Count Markov, and Prince Vyazemski — stopped coming to the club, meeting instead in private homes and intimate circles. Muscovites who took their cues from others — Ilya Rostov among them — were left without a clear opinion on the war and without leaders. Everyone felt that something was terribly wrong, and that discussing bad news was difficult, so silence seemed best. But after a while, like a jury emerging from deliberation, the opinion-makers reappeared, and everyone began speaking clearly and with conviction. Explanations were found for the incredible, unprecedented, and seemingly impossible event of a Russian defeat, and the same conclusions began circulating in every corner of Moscow. The causes were: Austrian treachery, a failing supply chain, the treachery of the Pole Przhebyshevski and the Frenchman Langeron, Kutuzov's incompetence, and — whispered quietly — the youth and inexperience of the Emperor, who had trusted worthless and insignificant advisers. But the army itself, the Russian army, everyone declared, had been extraordinary and had performed miracles of bravery. The soldiers, officers, and generals were all heroes. But the greatest hero of all was Prince Bagration, who had distinguished himself at Schon Grabern and during the retreat from Austerlitz, where he alone had withdrawn his column intact, holding off an enemy force twice his own size for an entire day. What also made Bagration Moscow's hero of choice was that he had no connections in the city and was a stranger there. In honoring him, they were paying tribute to a simple fighting Russian soldier without political connections or intrigues — a man associated through the Italian campaign with the great name of Suvorov. Moreover, celebrating Bagration was the perfect way to express disapproval of Kutuzov.

"If there had been no Bagration, it would have been necessary to invent him," said the wit Shinshin, riffing on Voltaire. No one spoke of Kutuzov except a few who cursed him in whispers, calling him a court weathervane and a dirty old man.

All Moscow repeated Prince Dolgorukov's quip: "If you keep kneading and kneading, you're bound to get your hands dirty" — offering the consolation of past victories to soften the present defeat. People also quoted Rostopchin's observation that French soldiers need lofty speeches to drive them into battle, Germans need logical arguments proving it's more dangerous to run away than to advance, but Russian soldiers simply need to be held back. Everywhere, new stories circulated about individual acts of heroism by Russian officers and soldiers at Austerlitz. One man had saved a regimental standard, another had killed five Frenchmen, a third had loaded five cannons single-handedly. People who didn't know Berg personally told how he had taken his sword in his left hand after being wounded in the right, and pressed forward. Of Bolkonsky, nothing was said, and only those who knew him personally mourned that he had died so young, leaving behind a pregnant wife and an eccentric father.

title: Book Four (1806) — Chapter 3
paragraphs: On that third of March, every room of the English Club buzzed with conversation, like bees swarming in spring. Members and guests wandered back and forth, sitting, standing, meeting, and separating — some in uniform, some in evening dress, and a few wearing powdered wigs and old-fashioned Russian kaftans. Powdered footmen in livery with buckled shoes and smart stockings stood at every door, anxiously tracking every visitor's movement so they could offer their services. Most of those present were elderly, respectable men with broad, self-assured faces, thick fingers, and decisive gestures and voices. This class of guests and members occupied their usual seats and gathered in their usual groups. A smaller portion were casual visitors — mostly young men, including Denisov, Rostov, and Dolokhov, who was now once again an officer in the Semenov regiment. The faces of these younger men, especially the military ones, wore an expression of polite condescension toward their elders that seemed to say, "We're happy to respect and honor you, but remember — the future belongs to us."

Nesvitski was there as a longtime club member. Pierre, who at his wife's insistence had let his hair grow and given up his spectacles, moved through the rooms in fashionable clothes but looking sad and listless. Here, as everywhere, he was surrounded by an atmosphere of deference to his wealth, and being accustomed to dominating such people, he treated them with distracted contempt.

By age he should have belonged to the younger set, but his wealth and connections placed him among the older, more distinguished guests, so he drifted from group to group. Some of the most prominent older men formed the centers of circles that even strangers approached respectfully to hear. The largest groups surrounded Count Rostopchin, Valuev, and Naryshkin. Rostopchin was describing how the Russians had been overrun by fleeing Austrians and had to cut through them with bayonets.
Valuev was confiding that Uvarov had been sent from Petersburg to find out what Moscow was thinking about Austerlitz.

In a third circle, Naryshkin was telling the story of how Suvorov had crowed like a rooster at an Austrian war council in response to the nonsense the Austrian generals were spouting. Shinshin, standing nearby, tried to crack a joke — saying Kutuzov had clearly failed to learn even that simple trick from Suvorov — but the senior members gave the wit a stern look, making him understand that in this place and on this occasion, it was inappropriate to speak that way about Kutuzov.

Count Ilya Rostov, hurried and preoccupied, bustled about in his soft-soled shoes between the dining room and drawing room, greeting important and unimportant guests alike — all of whom he knew — as if they were all equals, while his eyes kept searching for his fine, well-built young son, resting on him and winking at him happily. Young Rostov stood at a window with Dolokhov, whom he had recently met and whose company he greatly valued. The old count approached them and shook Dolokhov's hand.

"Please come visit us... you know my brave boy here... you were out there together... both playing the hero... Ah, Vasili Ignatovich... How are you, old friend?" he said, turning to a passing elderly man. But before he could finish his greeting, a general commotion broke out and a footman rushed in with a frightened face to announce: "He's arrived!"

Bells rang, the stewards hurried forward, and the guests — who had been scattered through different rooms like grain tossed in a shovel — poured together and crowded into the large drawing room by the ballroom entrance.

Bagration appeared in the anteroom doorway, without his hat or sword, which he had left with the porter as club custom required. He wore no lambskin cap and carried no loaded whip over his shoulder, as when Rostov had seen him on the eve of Austerlitz. Instead he wore a crisp new uniform with Russian and foreign decorations and the Star of St. George on his left breast. He had clearly just had his hair and whiskers trimmed for the occasion, which actually made him look slightly worse. There was something innocently festive about his appearance that, combined with his strong, masculine features, gave him a rather comical look. Bekleshev and Theodore Uvarov, who had arrived with him, paused at the doorway to let him enter first as guest of honor. Bagration was embarrassed by the courtesy and reluctant to accept it, which caused a brief delay at the door — but eventually he did enter first. He walked shyly and awkwardly across the parquet floor of the reception room, unsure what to do with his hands. He was far more comfortable walking across a plowed field under fire, as he had done leading the Kursk regiment at Schon Grabern — that would have been easier. The committee members met him at the first door and, expressing their delight at receiving such a distinguished guest, took charge of him without waiting for a reply, surrounded him, and led him to the drawing room. At first it was impossible to get through the drawing room door because of the crowd of members and guests jostling one another, each trying to get a good look at Bagration over the heads in front of them, as if he were some rare creature. Count Ilya Rostov, laughing and repeating, "Make way, my dear! Make way!" pushed through the crowd more energetically than anyone, led the guests into the drawing room, and seated them on the center sofa. The most important men and most respected members pressed around the new arrivals. Count Ilya pushed through the crowd again, left the drawing room, and returned a moment later with another committee member, carrying a large silver tray that he presented to Prince Bagration. On the tray lay verses composed and printed in the hero's honor. Bagration, seeing the tray, looked around in alarm as if searching for help. But every face demanded that he accept. He firmly took the tray with both hands and looked sternly, almost reproachfully, at the count who had presented it. Someone helpfully took the platter from him — otherwise he seemed prepared to carry it all evening and walk into dinner with it — and drew his attention to the verses.

"Very well, I'll read them then!" Bagration seemed to say, and fixing his weary eyes on the paper, he began reading with a fixed, serious expression. But the author himself took the verses and started reading them aloud. Bagration bowed his head and listened:

Bring glory then to Alexander's reign / And on the throne our Titus shield. / A dreaded foe be thou, kindhearted as a man, / A Rhipheus at home, a Caesar in the field! / E'en fortunate Napoleon / Knows by experience, now, Bagration, / And dare not Herculean Russians trouble...
But before the reading was finished, a booming major-domo announced that dinner was served! The door opened, and from the dining room came the resounding strains of a polonaise:
Conquest's joyful thunder waken, / Triumph, valiant Russians, now!...

Count Rostov, glancing irritably at the author who was still reading his verses, bowed to Bagration. Everyone stood, recognizing that dinner mattered more than poetry, and Bagration once again led the way in. He was seated in the place of honor between two men named Alexander — Bekleshev and Naryshkin — a meaningful nod to the Emperor's name. Three hundred people took their seats according to rank and importance, the most distinguished sitting closest to the guest of honor, as naturally as water flows to the lowest ground.

Just before dinner, Count Ilya Rostov introduced his son to Bagration, who recognized him and said a few words — halting and awkward, like everything he said that day. Count Ilya beamed with pride as Bagration spoke to his son.

Nicholas Rostov sat with Denisov and his new acquaintance Dolokhov near the middle of the table. Across from them sat Pierre, next to Prince Nesvitski. Count Ilya Rostov, along with the other committee members, sat facing Bagration and, as the very embodiment of Moscow hospitality, served as the prince's host.

His efforts had not been wasted. The dinner — both the Lenten dishes and the regular fare — was magnificent, yet he couldn't relax until the meal was over. He kept winking at the butler, whispering instructions to the footmen, and awaiting each course with visible anxiety. Everything was superb. With the second course, an enormous sterlet — the sight of which made Ilya Rostov blush with self-conscious pleasure — the footmen began popping champagne corks and filling glasses. After the fish, which caused quite a stir, the count exchanged looks with the other committee members. "There'll be many toasts — it's time to start," he whispered, and raising his glass, he stood up. Everyone fell silent, waiting for what he would say.

"To the health of our Sovereign, the Emperor!" he cried, and at that moment his kind eyes glistened with tears of joy and emotion. The band instantly struck up "Conquest's joyful thunder waken..." Everyone rose and shouted "Hurrah!" Bagration also stood and shouted "Hurrah!" in exactly the same voice he had used on the battlefield at Schon Grabern. Young Rostov's ecstatic voice rang out above the three hundred others. He nearly wept. "To the health of our Sovereign, the Emperor!" he roared, "Hurrah!" He drained his glass in one gulp and smashed it on the floor. Many followed his example, and the loud cheering went on for a long time. When the noise died down, the footmen swept away the broken glass and everyone sat down again, smiling at the racket they had made and exchanging remarks. The old count stood up again, glanced at a note beside his plate, and proposed another toast: "To the health of the hero of our last campaign, Prince Pyotr Ivanovich Bagration!" His blue eyes filled with tears once more. "Hurrah!" the three hundred voices cried again. But this time, instead of the band, a choir began singing a cantata composed by Pavel Ivanovich Kutuzov:
Russians! O'er all barriers on! / Courage conquest guarantees; / Have we not Bagration? / He brings foemen to their knees...

As soon as the singing ended, one toast followed another. Count Ilya Rostov grew more and more emotional, more glasses were smashed, and the cheering grew louder. They drank to Bekleshev, Naryshkin, Uvarov, Dolgorukov, Apraksin, Valuev, the committee, all the club members, and all the club guests — and finally to Count Ilya Rostov himself, as the organizer of the banquet. At that toast, the count pulled out his handkerchief, covered his face, and wept openly.

title: Book Four (1806) — Chapter 4
paragraphs: Pierre sat across from Dolokhov and Nicholas Rostov. As usual, he ate and drank heavily. But those who knew him well could see that some great change had come over him that day. He was silent throughout dinner, looking around while blinking and frowning, or else staring into space with complete absent-mindedness, rubbing the bridge of his nose. His face was gloomy and troubled. He seemed to see and hear nothing happening around him, entirely absorbed by some painful, unresolved problem.

The problem tormenting him had been set in motion by hints from the princess — his cousin — in Moscow, regarding Dolokhov's intimacy with his wife, and by an anonymous letter he had received that morning. The letter, written in the typically crude and mocking style of such messages, said that he couldn't see well through his spectacles, but that his wife's affair with Dolokhov was a secret to no one but him. Pierre categorically refused to believe either the princess's hints or the letter, but he now dreaded looking at Dolokhov, who sat right across from him. Every time he accidentally met Dolokhov's handsome, insolent eyes, Pierre felt something terrible and monstrous rising in his soul and quickly turned away. Involuntarily recalling his wife's past and her relationship with Dolokhov, Pierre could see clearly that what the letter described might be true — or at least could appear true — if it hadn't been about his own wife. He couldn't help remembering how Dolokhov, who had fully recovered his former standing after the campaign, had returned to Petersburg and come to him. Taking advantage of their friendship as drinking companions, Dolokhov had moved straight into Pierre's house, and Pierre had put him up and lent him money. Pierre recalled how Helene had smiled disapprovingly at Dolokhov living with them, and how Dolokhov had brazenly complimented Pierre on his wife's beauty — and from that point on, all the way to Moscow, had never left them for a single day.

"Yes, he's very handsome," thought Pierre, "and I know his character. It would give him special pleasure to dishonor my name and humiliate me, precisely because I've gone out of my way for him — befriended him, helped him. I know and understand how much extra relish that would add to the pleasure of deceiving me, if it were really true. Yes, if it were true — but I don't believe it. I have no right to believe it, and I can't." He remembered the expression Dolokhov's face took on in moments of cruelty — when he had tied a policeman to a bear and dropped them into the water, when he had challenged a man to a duel for no reason, when he had shot a coachman's horse with a pistol. That expression was often on Dolokhov's face when he looked at Pierre. "Yes, he's a thug," thought Pierre. "Killing a man means nothing to him. He must think everyone's afraid of him, and that must please him. He probably thinks I'm afraid of him too — and in fact, I am." And again he felt something terrible and monstrous rising within him. Dolokhov, Denisov, and Rostov were sitting across from Pierre and seemed to be in high spirits. Rostov was talking cheerfully with his two friends — one a dashing hussar, the other a notorious duelist and libertine — and he kept glancing mockingly at Pierre, whose preoccupied, distracted, and massive figure was quite conspicuous at the dinner. Rostov regarded Pierre with hostility — first, because in a hussar's eyes Pierre was merely a rich civilian married to a beauty, in other words, an old woman; and second, because Pierre, lost in his own thoughts, hadn't recognized Rostov or returned his greeting. When the toast to the Emperor's health was drunk, Pierre, deep in thought, didn't stand or raise his glass.
"What are you doing?" shouted Rostov, staring at him in an ecstasy of indignation. "Don't you hear? It's His Majesty the Emperor's health!"
Pierre sighed, stood up obediently, emptied his glass, and after everyone had sat down again, turned to Rostov with his usual kind smile.
"I'm sorry — I didn't recognize you!" he said. But Rostov was already occupied with something else — he was shouting "Hurrah!"
"Why don't you go reintroduce yourself?" said Dolokhov to Rostov.
"Forget him — he's an idiot," said Rostov.
"One should make an effort with the husbands of pretty women," said Denisov.
Pierre didn't catch what they were saying, but he knew they were talking about him. He turned red and looked away.
"Well then — to the health of beautiful women!" said Dolokhov, and with a serious expression but a smile lurking at the corners of his mouth, he raised his glass toward Pierre.
"To the health of lovely women, my dear Petrusha — and their lovers!" he added.

Pierre, eyes downcast, drained his glass without looking at Dolokhov or responding. A footman distributing copies of Kutuzov's cantata placed one in front of Pierre as one of the principal guests. He was about to pick it up when Dolokhov leaned across the table and snatched it from his hand, starting to read it. Pierre stared at Dolokhov, and his eyes darkened. The terrible, monstrous thing that had been tormenting him all through dinner surged up and took hold of him. He heaved his massive body across the table.
"How dare you take that!" he shouted.
Hearing that shout and seeing who it was directed at, Nesvitski and the man sitting beside Pierre turned to him in alarm.
"Stop! Stop! What are you doing?" came their frightened whispers.
Dolokhov looked at Pierre with clear, amused, cruel eyes, wearing that smile of his that seemed to say, "Ah, now this is what I enjoy."
"You won't have it," he said distinctly.
Pierre, white-faced, his lips trembling, grabbed the copy back.
"You... you... scoundrel! I challenge you!" he burst out, and shoving back his chair, he rose from the table.

At the very instant he said those words, Pierre felt that the question of his wife's guilt — which had been torturing him all day — was finally and conclusively answered: yes, she was guilty. He hated her and was forever separated from her. Despite Denisov's plea that he stay out of it, Rostov agreed to serve as Dolokhov's second. After dinner, he discussed the arrangements for the duel with Nesvitski, who was Pierre's second. Pierre went home, but Rostov, Dolokhov, and Denisov stayed on at the club until late, listening to the gypsy singers and other performers.
"So then — tomorrow at Sokolniki," said Dolokhov, taking leave of Rostov at the club entrance.
"And you feel completely calm?" Rostov asked.
Dolokhov paused.

"I'll tell you the whole secret of dueling in two words. If you're going to fight a duel and you sit down to write your will and tender letters to your parents, thinking you might be killed — you're a fool and you're done for. But if you go with the firm intention of killing your opponent as quickly and surely as possible, then everything will be fine. That's what our bear hunter back in Kostroma used to tell me: 'Everyone's afraid of a bear,' he'd say, 'but once you see one, all your fear vanishes — your only thought is not to let him get away!' That's how it is with me. À demain, mon cher."
* Till tomorrow, my dear fellow.

The next morning, at eight o'clock, Pierre and Nesvitski drove to the Sokolniki forest, where they found Dolokhov, Denisov, and Rostov already waiting. Pierre had the look of a man consumed by thoughts that had nothing to do with the matter at hand. His drawn face was sallow. He had obviously not slept. He kept looking around distractedly and squinting as if dazzled by the sun. He was entirely preoccupied with two thoughts: his wife's guilt, of which he no longer had the slightest doubt after his sleepless night, and the blamelessness of Dolokhov, who had no reason to protect the honor of a man who meant nothing to him. "I would probably have done the same in his place," Pierre thought. "Actually, I'm sure I would have. So why this duel? Why this killing? Either I'll kill him, or he'll hit me in the head, or the elbow, or the knee. Why can't I just leave — run away — disappear somewhere?" Such thoughts kept passing through his mind. But at those very moments he would ask, in a particularly calm, distracted tone that earned the respect of the onlookers, "Will this take much longer? Is everything ready?"
When everything was prepared — the sabers planted in the snow to mark the barriers and the pistols loaded — Nesvitski walked up to Pierre.

"I would not be doing my duty, Count," he said in a timid voice, "and would not deserve the confidence and honor you've shown me by choosing me as your second, if at this grave — this very grave — moment, I did not tell you the whole truth. I believe there are no sufficient grounds for this affair, and no reason for blood to be shed. You were not entirely right — you were impulsive..."
"Oh yes, it's horribly stupid," said Pierre.

"Then allow me to convey your regrets, and I'm sure your opponent will accept them," said Nesvitski, who, like everyone else involved — and like everyone in such situations — still couldn't quite believe it had come to an actual duel. "You know, Count, it's far more honorable to admit a mistake than to let things become irreparable. There was no real insult on either side. Let me speak to them..."
"No! What is there to discuss?" said Pierre. "It doesn't matter.... Is everything ready?" he added. "Just tell me where to stand and where to aim." He said this with an unnaturally gentle smile.
He took the pistol and began asking how the trigger worked, since he had never held a pistol before — a fact he didn't want to admit.
"Oh yes, that's right — I know. I just forgot," he said.
"No apologies — none whatsoever," said Dolokhov to Denisov, who had been attempting a reconciliation on his side. Then Dolokhov too walked to his appointed place.

The spot chosen for the duel was about eighty paces from the road where the sleighs had been left — a small clearing in the pine forest, covered in melting snow, the frost having broken during the past few days. The two men stood forty paces apart at the far edge of the clearing. The seconds paced out the distance, leaving tracks in the deep, wet snow between the starting positions and the two sabers stuck in the ground ten paces apart to mark the barriers. The air was damp and misty. At forty paces, nothing could be seen clearly. For three minutes everything had been ready, but still they delayed, and everyone was silent.

title: Book Four (1806) — Chapter 5
paragraphs: "Well, begin!" said Dolokhov.

"All right," said Pierre, still wearing the same smile. A feeling of dread hung in the air. It was clear that this affair, so casually begun, could no longer be stopped — it was taking its own course, beyond anyone's control.
Denisov went first to the barrier and announced: "As the adversaries have refused a reconciliation, please proceed. Take your pistols, and at the word three, begin to advance."
"One! Two! Three!" he shouted angrily, and stepped aside.

The two men advanced along the trampled paths, drawing closer and closer, beginning to make each other out through the mist. They were free to fire whenever they chose as they approached the barrier. Dolokhov walked slowly without raising his pistol, his bright, sparkling blue eyes fixed intently on his opponent's face. His mouth wore its usual hint of a smile.

"So I can fire whenever I want!" said Pierre, and at the word "three" he walked quickly forward, missing the trampled path and stepping into deep snow. He held the pistol in his outstretched right hand, apparently afraid of shooting himself with it. He kept his left hand carefully behind him, because he wanted to steady his right hand with it but knew he wasn't supposed to. After advancing six paces and straying off the path into the snow, Pierre glanced down at his feet, then quickly looked up at Dolokhov and, bending his finger as he'd been shown, fired. Not at all expecting such a loud report, Pierre flinched at the sound and then, smiling at his own reaction, stood still. The smoke, made denser by the mist, blocked his view for a moment, but there was no second shot as he had expected. He only heard Dolokhov's hurried steps, and then his figure emerged through the smoke. He was pressing one hand to his left side while the other clutched his drooping pistol. His face was pale. Rostov ran toward him and said something.

"N-no!" Dolokhov muttered through clenched teeth. "No, it's not over." And after stumbling a few staggering steps right up to the saber marker, he collapsed onto the snow beside it. His left hand was bloody; he wiped it on his coat and propped himself up with it. His frowning face was deathly pale and trembling.
"Plea—" Dolokhov began, but couldn't get the word out at first.
"Please," he managed with effort.
Pierre, barely holding back his sobs, started running toward Dolokhov and was about to cross the space between the barriers when Dolokhov shouted:

"Back to your barrier!" Pierre understood what was meant and stopped by his saber. Only ten paces separated them. Dolokhov lowered his head to the snow and bit at it hungrily, then raised his head again, adjusted his position, drew in his legs, and sat up, searching for a firm center of gravity. He sucked and swallowed the cold snow; his lips quivered, but his eyes, still smiling, glittered with effort and fury as he summoned his remaining strength. He raised his pistol and took aim.
"Sideways! Shield yourself with your pistol!" shouted Nesvitski.
"Take cover!" even Denisov cried out to his opponent.

Pierre, with a gentle smile of pity and remorse, his arms and legs spread helplessly, stood with his broad chest facing Dolokhov directly and looked at him with sorrow. Denisov, Rostov, and Nesvitski squeezed their eyes shut. At that same instant they heard a shot and Dolokhov's furious cry.
"Missed!" Dolokhov shouted, and he lay helplessly face down in the snow.
Pierre clutched his temples and, turning around, walked into the forest, trampling through the deep snow and muttering incoherent words:
"Madness... madness! Death... lies..." he repeated, his face contorted.
Nesvitski stopped him and took him home.
Rostov and Denisov drove away with the wounded Dolokhov.

Dolokhov lay silent in the sleigh with his eyes closed, not answering any of the questions put to him. But as they entered Moscow he suddenly came to and, lifting his head with effort, took hold of Rostov's hand — Rostov was sitting beside him. Rostov was struck by the completely altered, unexpectedly tender and emotional expression on Dolokhov's face.
"Well? How do you feel?" he asked.

"Bad! But that's not it, my friend —" said Dolokhov in a gasping voice. "Where are we? In Moscow, I know. I don't matter, but I've killed her, killed... She won't recover from this! She won't survive...."
"Who?" asked Rostov.
"My mother! My mother, my angel, my beloved angel mother," and Dolokhov squeezed Rostov's hand and burst into tears.
When he had calmed down a little, he explained to Rostov that he was living with his mother, who, if she saw him dying, would not survive it. He begged Rostov to go ahead and prepare her.

Rostov went on ahead to do as asked, and to his great surprise learned that Dolokhov the brawler, Dolokhov the bully, lived in Moscow with an elderly mother and a hunchbacked sister, and was the most devoted of sons and brothers.

title: Book Four (1806) — Chapter 6
paragraphs: Pierre had rarely seen his wife alone lately. Both in Petersburg and in Moscow their house was always full of guests. The night after the duel he didn't go to his bedroom but instead, as he often did, stayed in his father's room — that enormous room where Count Bezukhov had died.

He lay down on the sofa intending to fall asleep and forget everything that had happened, but he couldn't. Such a storm of feelings, thoughts, and memories suddenly overwhelmed him that he couldn't sleep or even stay in one place. He had to jump up and pace the room with rapid steps. One moment he seemed to see her in the early days of their marriage, with bare shoulders and a languid, passionate expression on her face, and then immediately he saw beside her Dolokhov's handsome, insolent, hard, and mocking face as it had been at the banquet — and then that same face, pale, trembling, and suffering, as it had looked when he staggered and sank into the snow.

"What has happened?" he asked himself. "I've killed her lover — yes, killed my wife's lover. Yes, that's what happened! And why? How did I come to do it?" — "Because you married her," answered an inner voice.

"But how was I to blame?" he asked. "For marrying her without loving her; for deceiving yourself and her." And he vividly recalled that moment after supper at Prince Vasili's when he had spoken those words he found so hard to say: "I love you." "It all comes from that! Even then I felt it," he thought. "I felt then that it wasn't right, that I had no right to do it. And so it has turned out."

He remembered his honeymoon and blushed at the memory. One recollection was particularly vivid, humiliating, and shameful — how one day, shortly after his marriage, he had come out of the bedroom into his study a little before noon in his silk dressing gown, and found his head steward there. The man bowed respectfully, glanced at his face and his dressing gown, and smiled slightly, as if expressing a tactful understanding of his master's happiness.

"But how often I was proud of her — proud of her majestic beauty and social skill," he thought. "I was proud of my house, where she entertained all of Petersburg, proud of her cool composure and beauty. So this is what I was proud of! Back then I thought I didn't understand her. How often, when thinking about her character, I told myself that I was the one at fault for not understanding her, for not understanding that constant poise and self-satisfaction and complete lack of interests or desires. And the whole secret lies in the terrible truth that she is a corrupt woman. Now I've said that terrible word to myself, everything has become clear."

"Anatole used to come to borrow money from her and would kiss her bare shoulders. She didn't give him the money but let herself be kissed. Her father once tried, as a joke, to make her jealous, and she replied with a calm smile that she wasn't stupid enough to be jealous. 'Let him do what he wants,' she used to say about me. One day I asked her if she had any signs of pregnancy. She laughed scornfully and said she wasn't fool enough to want children, and that she wasn't going to have any children by me."
Then he recalled the coarseness and bluntness of her thoughts and the vulgarity of her expressions, despite her aristocratic upbringing.
