"'I'm not that stupid.... Just you try.... Get lost,' she used to say. Seeing how successful she was with young and old men and women, Pierre often couldn't understand why he didn't love her.
* "Get lost."

"Yes, I never loved her," he said to himself. "I knew she was a corrupt woman," he repeated, "but I didn't dare admit it to myself. And now Dolokhov is sitting in the snow with a forced smile, perhaps dying, while I face my remorse with some kind of forced bravado!"
Pierre was one of those people who, despite appearing to have what's called a weak character, don't seek a confidant when they're in trouble. He processed his suffering alone.

"It's all her fault," he told himself. "But what does that matter? Why did I tie myself to her? Why did I say 'I love you' to her — which was a lie, and worse than a lie? I'm guilty and must endure... what? A stain on my name? A lifelong misfortune? Oh, that's nonsense," he thought. "A stain on my name and honor — that's something separate from who I really am."
* I love you.

"Louis XVI was executed because they said he was dishonorable and a criminal," the thought came to Pierre. "And from their point of view, they were right — just as those were right who made him a saint and died as martyrs for his sake. Then Robespierre was beheaded for being a tyrant. Who is right and who is wrong? No one! But if you're alive — live. Tomorrow you'll die, just as I might have died an hour ago. And is it worth tormenting yourself when you have only a moment of life compared to eternity?"

But the moment he imagined himself calmed by such thoughts, she suddenly came into his mind as she had been in those moments when he'd most strongly expressed his fake love for her, and he felt the blood rush to his heart and had to get up again and move around and smash and tear at whatever came to hand. "Why did I tell her 'I love you'?" he kept repeating to himself. And after saying it for the tenth time, Moliere's words came to him: "But what the devil was he doing in that boat?" — and he began to laugh at himself.
* "But what the devil was he doing in that boat?"

During the night he called his valet and told him to pack for Petersburg. He couldn't imagine how he could face her now. He decided to leave the next day and write her a letter informing her of his intention to separate from her forever.
The next morning, when the valet came in with coffee, Pierre was lying asleep on the ottoman with an open book in his hand.
He woke up and looked around for a while with a startled expression, unable to grasp where he was.
"The countess asked me to inquire whether your excellency was at home," said the valet.

But before Pierre could decide what answer to send, the countess herself entered the room. She wore a white satin dressing gown embroidered with silver, her hair simply arranged — two thick braids wound twice around her lovely head like a crown. She was calm and majestic, except for an angry crease on her rather prominent marble forehead. With unshakable composure she didn't speak in front of the valet. She knew about the duel and had come to discuss it. She waited until the valet had set down the coffee things and left. Pierre looked at her timidly over his spectacles, like a hare that, surrounded by hounds, flattens its ears and crouches motionless before its enemies — he tried to go on reading. But realizing this was pointless and impossible, he glanced at her timidly again. She didn't sit down but stood looking at him with a contemptuous smile, waiting for the valet to leave.
"Well, what's this about? What have you been up to now, I'd like to know?" she asked sternly.
"Me? What have I...?" Pierre stammered.
"So you're a hero now, are you? Come on, what was this duel about? What is it supposed to prove? What? I'm asking you."
Pierre rolled over heavily on the ottoman and opened his mouth but couldn't reply.

"If you won't answer, I'll tell you myself..." Helene continued. "You believe everything people tell you. You were told" — Helene laughed — "that Dolokhov was my lover," she said with her characteristic blunt directness, tossing out the word as casually as any other, "and you believed it! Well, what have you proved? What does this duel prove? That you're a fool — but everybody already knew that. What's going to happen now? I'll be the laughingstock of all Moscow. Everyone will say that you, drunk and clueless about what you were doing, challenged a man you were jealous of for no reason." Helene's voice rose and she grew more and more agitated. "A man who is better than you in every way..."
"Hmm... hmm..." Pierre growled, frowning without looking at her and not moving a muscle.
"And how could you believe he was my lover? Why? Because I enjoy his company? If you were more intelligent and more pleasant, I'd prefer yours."
"Don't talk to me... please," Pierre muttered hoarsely.
"Why shouldn't I talk? I can say whatever I want, and I'll tell you plainly that very few wives with husbands like you would have avoided taking lovers — but I haven't done that," she said.

Pierre wanted to say something. He looked at her with a strange expression she didn't understand, then lay down again. He was in physical agony at that moment — there was a weight on his chest and he couldn't breathe. He knew he had to do something to end this suffering, but what he wanted to do was too terrible.
"We should separate," he muttered in a broken voice.
"Separate? Fine, but only if you give me a fortune," said Helene. "Separate! As if that's supposed to scare me!"
Pierre leaped up from the sofa and rushed staggering toward her.
"I'll kill you!" he shouted, and seizing the marble top of a table with a strength he'd never felt before, he took a step toward her, brandishing the heavy slab.

Helene's face became terrified. She shrieked and sprang aside. His father's nature showed itself in Pierre. He felt the thrill and ecstasy of rage. He hurled down the marble slab, shattering it, and lunging toward her with outstretched hands, he roared "Get out!" in such a terrible voice that the whole house heard it with horror. God knows what he would have done if Helene hadn't fled the room.
A week later Pierre gave his wife full control over all his estates in central Russia, which made up the greater part of his wealth, and left for Petersburg alone.

title: Book Four (1806) — Chapter 7
paragraphs: Two months had passed since news of the Battle of Austerlitz and the loss of Prince Andrew had reached Bald Hills. Despite letters sent through the embassy and extensive searches, his body had not been found, nor was he on any list of prisoners. Worst of all for his family was the lingering possibility that he had been picked up on the battlefield by local people and might now be lying somewhere, recovering or dying, alone among strangers, unable to send word. The official newspapers, from which the old prince first learned of the defeat at Austerlitz, reported — as usual very briefly and vaguely — that after brilliant engagements the Russians had been forced to retreat and had done so in perfect order. The old prince understood from this report that the army had been defeated. A week after the newspaper account of the battle, a letter arrived from Kutuzov informing the prince of what had befallen his son.

"Your son," Kutuzov wrote, "fell before my eyes, a standard in his hand, at the head of a regiment — he fell as a hero, worthy of his father and his fatherland. To my great regret and that of the whole army, it is still uncertain whether he is alive or not. I take comfort, and offer it to you, in the hope that your son is alive, since otherwise he would have been listed among the officers found on the battlefield — a list which has been sent to me under a flag of truce."

After receiving this news late in the evening, when he was alone in his study, the old prince went for his walk as usual the next morning. But he was silent with his steward, the gardener, and the architect, and though he looked very stern, he said nothing to anyone.
When Princess Mary came to him at the usual hour, he was working at his lathe and, as always, didn't look up when she entered.

"Ah, Princess Mary!" he suddenly said in an unnatural voice, throwing down his chisel. The wheel continued spinning by its own momentum, and Princess Mary would always remember the dying creak of that wheel, which merged in her memory with everything that followed.

She went up to him, saw his face, and something broke inside her. Her eyes grew dim. From the expression on her father's face — not sad, not broken, but angry and working unnaturally — she could see that some terrible catastrophe was hanging over her and about to crush her. The worst thing in life, something she had never experienced — irreparable and incomprehensible — the death of someone she loved.
"Father! Andrew!" said the plain, awkward princess with such indescribable beauty of grief and selflessness that her father couldn't bear her look and turned away with a sob.
"Bad news! He's not among the prisoners or the dead! Kutuzov writes..." and he let out a piercing scream, as if trying to drive the princess away with it. "Killed!"

The princess didn't collapse or faint. She was already pale, but when she heard these words, her face changed and something lit up in her beautiful, radiant eyes. It was as if a supreme joy — a joy beyond the joys and sorrows of this world — flooded over the immense grief within her. She forgot all fear of her father, went up to him, took his hand, and drawing him down, put her arm around his thin, bony neck.
"Father," she said, "don't turn away from me. Let us cry together."
"Scoundrels! Villains!" the old man shrieked, turning his face away from her. "Destroying the army, destroying men! And for what? Go — go and tell Lise."

The princess sank helplessly into an armchair beside her father and wept. She saw her brother as he had been at the moment he said goodbye to her and to Lise — his expression tender yet proud. She saw him tender and amused as he had been when he put on the little icon. "Did he believe? Had he repented of his doubt? Was he there now? There, in the realm of eternal peace and blessedness?" she wondered.
"Father, tell me how it happened," she asked through her tears.
"Go! Go! Killed in battle, where the finest Russian men and Russia's glory were led to destruction. Go, Princess Mary. Go and tell Lise. I'll follow."

When Princess Mary returned from her father, the little princess sat doing needlework, looking up with that curious expression of inner, happy calm that is unique to pregnant women. It was clear that her eyes didn't see Princess Mary — they were looking inward, into herself, at something joyful and mysterious happening within her.
"Mary," she said, pushing away from the embroidery frame and leaning back, "give me your hand." She took her sister-in-law's hand and placed it below her waist.
Her eyes smiled with anticipation; her soft, downy lip lifted and stayed raised in childlike happiness.
Princess Mary knelt before her and buried her face in the folds of her sister-in-law's dress.
"There — there! Do you feel it? It's such a strange feeling. And you know, Mary, I'm going to love him so much," said Lise, gazing at her sister-in-law with bright, happy eyes.
Princess Mary couldn't lift her head. She was crying.
"What's the matter, Mary?"
"Nothing... it's just that I feel sad... sad about Andrew," she said, wiping her tears on her sister-in-law's knee.

Several times that morning Princess Mary tried to prepare her sister-in-law for the news, but each time she started, she began to cry. Unobservant as the little princess was, these tears, whose cause she didn't understand, unsettled her. She said nothing but glanced around uneasily, as if searching for something. Before dinner the old prince, of whom she was always afraid, came into her room with a particularly restless and hostile expression, then left again without a word. She looked at Princess Mary, then sat thinking for a while with that look of inward attention seen only in pregnant women, and suddenly began to cry.
"Has there been any word from Andrew?" she asked.
"No — you know it's too soon for news. But Father is worried, and I'm frightened."
"So there's nothing?"
"Nothing," answered Princess Mary, looking firmly at her sister-in-law with her radiant eyes.

She had resolved not to tell her and had persuaded her father to hide the terrible news until after the birth, which was expected any day. Princess Mary and the old prince each bore and concealed their grief in their own way. The old prince refused to hold out any hope. He made up his mind that Prince Andrew had been killed, and although he sent an official to Austria to search for traces of his son, he ordered a monument from Moscow that he planned to erect in his own garden as a memorial, and he told everyone that his son had been killed. He tried not to change his usual routine, but his strength was failing. He walked less, ate less, slept less, and grew weaker every day. Princess Mary held onto hope. She prayed for her brother as for a living man and was constantly waiting for news of his return.

title: Book Four (1806) — Chapter 8
paragraphs: "Darling," said the little princess after breakfast on the morning of the nineteenth of March, and her downy little lip rose from old habit. But since sorrow now colored every smile, every word, and even every footstep in that house after the terrible news had arrived, the little princess's smile — though she didn't know the cause of the sadness around her — only served as another reminder of the general grief.
"Darling, I'm afraid this morning's breakfast — or fruschtique, as Foka the cook calls it — hasn't agreed with me."
* Fruhstuck: breakfast.
"What's wrong, sweetheart? You look pale. Oh, you're very pale!" said Princess Mary in alarm, hurrying over to her sister-in-law with her soft, heavy steps.

"Your excellency, shouldn't we send for Mary Bogdanovna?" said one of the maids who was present. Mary Bogdanovna was a midwife from the nearby town who had been staying at Bald Hills for the past two weeks.
"Oh yes," agreed Princess Mary. "Perhaps that's what it is. I'll go. Be brave, my angel." She kissed Lise and was about to leave the room.
"Oh, no, no!" And beyond the pallor and physical discomfort on the little princess's face, there appeared an expression of childlike terror at the prospect of unavoidable pain.

"No, it's just indigestion... Say it's only indigestion, say so, Mary! Say it..." And the little princess began crying like a suffering child, wringing her small hands with something almost theatrical in the gesture. Princess Mary rushed out of the room to fetch Mary Bogdanovna.
"My God! My God! Oh!" she heard as she left.
The midwife was already on her way to meet her, rubbing her small, plump white hands with an air of calm self-assurance.
"Mary Bogdanovna, I think it's starting!" said Princess Mary, her eyes wide with alarm.
"Well, the Lord be praised, Princess," said Mary Bogdanovna without hurrying. "You young ladies really don't need to know about these things."

"But why hasn't the doctor from Moscow arrived yet?" asked the princess. In keeping with Lise's and Prince Andrew's wishes, they had sent to Moscow for a doctor well in advance, and were expecting him at any moment.
"It doesn't matter, Princess. Don't be alarmed," said Mary Bogdanovna. "We'll manage perfectly well without a doctor."

Five minutes later, from her room, Princess Mary heard something heavy being carried past. She looked out. The servants were carrying the large leather sofa from Prince Andrew's study into the bedroom. Their faces wore a quiet, solemn expression.

Princess Mary sat alone in her room, listening to the sounds of the house, occasionally opening her door when someone passed and watching the activity in the corridor. Women went quietly in and out of the bedroom, glancing at the princess and turning away. She didn't dare ask any questions and closed her door again, sometimes sitting in her armchair, sometimes picking up her prayer book, sometimes kneeling before the icon stand. To her surprise and distress, she found that prayer did not calm her agitation. Suddenly her door opened softly and her old nurse, Praskovya Savishna — who almost never came to that part of the house because the old prince had forbidden it — appeared on the threshold with a shawl around her head.
"I've come to sit with you a bit, Masha," said the nurse, "and look, I've brought the prince's wedding candles to light before his icon, my angel," she added with a sigh.
"Oh, nurse, I'm so glad!"
"God is merciful, my dear."

The nurse lit the gilded candles before the icons and sat down by the door with her knitting. Princess Mary picked up a book and began to read. Only when they heard footsteps or voices did the two women look at each other — the princess anxious and questioning, the nurse reassuring. Everyone in the house felt the same thing Princess Mary was feeling in her room. But because of the old belief that the fewer people who know about it, the less a woman in labor suffers, everyone pretended to be unaware. No one spoke of it, yet beneath the usual composed and respectful manners of the prince's household, there was a shared sense of anxiety, a softening of hearts, and a feeling that something great and mysterious was taking place.

There was no laughter in the maids' large hall. In the men servants' quarters, everyone sat waiting — silent and alert. In the outer servants' lodgings, torches and candles burned and no one slept. The old prince, pacing his study on his heels, sent Tikhon to ask Mary Bogdanovna for news. "Just say 'the prince asked me to inquire' — and come tell me her answer."
"Please inform the prince that labor has begun," said Mary Bogdanovna, giving the messenger a meaningful look.
Tikhon went and told the prince.
"Very good!" said the prince, closing the door behind him. After that, Tikhon heard not the slightest sound from the study.

After a while he went back in as if to trim the candles, and seeing the prince lying on the sofa, looked at him, noticed his troubled face, shook his head, and going up to him, silently kissed him on the shoulder and left the room — without trimming the candles and without explaining why he'd come. The most sacred mystery in the world continued to unfold. Evening passed, night came, and the feeling of suspense and tenderness before the unknowable did not lessen but grew stronger. No one slept.

It was one of those March nights when winter seems determined to reclaim its hold, scattering its last snows and storms with desperate fury. A relay of fresh horses had been sent to the highway to meet the German doctor traveling from Moscow, who was expected at any moment, and men on horseback with lanterns had been dispatched to the crossroads to guide him over the country road with its ruts and snow-covered puddles.

Princess Mary had long since set aside her book. She sat in silence, her luminous eyes fixed on her nurse's wrinkled face — every line of which she knew so well — on the strand of gray hair escaping from under the kerchief, and on the loose skin hanging beneath her chin.

Nurse Savishna, knitting in hand, was telling in low tones — barely hearing or understanding her own words — the story she had told hundreds of times before: how the late princess had given birth to Princess Mary in Kishinev with only a Moldavian peasant woman to help, instead of a proper midwife.
"God is merciful — doctors are never needed," she said.

Suddenly a gust of wind slammed against the casement window, from which the inner frame had been removed — as per the prince's standing order to remove one window frame in each room as soon as the larks returned. The gust forced open the loosely fastened latch, set the damask curtain flapping, and blew out the candle with its cold, snowy draft. Princess Mary shuddered. Her nurse set down her knitting, went to the window, and leaned out to catch the swinging casement. The cold wind whipped the ends of her kerchief and her loose strands of gray hair.
"Princess, my dear — there's someone coming up the drive!" she said, still holding the casement open. "With lanterns. Most likely the doctor."
"Oh, thank God! Thank God!" said Princess Mary. "I must go meet him — he doesn't speak Russian."

Princess Mary threw a shawl over her head and ran to meet the new arrival. As she crossed the front hall, she could see through the window a carriage with lanterns standing at the entrance. She went out onto the stairs. On a banister post stood a tallow candle guttering in the draft. On the landing below, Philip the footman stood looking frightened, holding another candle. Still lower, beyond the turn of the staircase, she could hear footsteps in thick felt boots, and a voice that sounded familiar to Princess Mary was saying something.
"Thank God!" said the voice. "And Father?"
"Gone to bed," replied the voice of Demyan the house steward from below.
Then the voice said something more, Demyan answered, and the footsteps in felt boots came more rapidly up toward the unseen bend of the staircase.

"It's Andrew!" thought Princess Mary. "No, it can't be — that would be too extraordinary." And at the very moment she thought this, the face and figure of Prince Andrew appeared on the landing where the footman stood with the candle. He wore a fur cloak with a deep collar covered in snow. Yes, it was him — pale, thin, with a changed and strangely softened but agitated expression on his face. He climbed the stairs and embraced his sister.

"You didn't get my letter?" he asked, and without waiting for a reply — which he wouldn't have received anyway, since the princess was unable to speak — he turned back, quickly went down the stairs again with the doctor who had come in after him (they had met at the last post station), and then came back up and embraced his sister again.
"What a strange twist of fate, Masha darling!" And having taken off his cloak and felt boots, he went to the little princess's room.

title: Book Four (1806) — Chapter 9
paragraphs: The little princess lay propped up on pillows, a white cap on her head — the contractions had just stopped for the moment. Strands of her black hair clung to her flushed, perspiring cheeks. Her lovely rosy mouth with its downy lip was open and she was smiling happily. Prince Andrew came in and stopped at the foot of the sofa where she lay. Her shining eyes, filled with childlike fear and excitement, rested on him without changing expression. "I love everyone and have never harmed anyone — so why must I suffer like this? Help me!" her look seemed to say. She saw her husband but didn't grasp what his appearance here and now really meant. Prince Andrew walked around the sofa and kissed her forehead.
"My darling!" he said — a word he had never used with her before. "God is merciful...."
She looked at him with an inquiring, childlike reproach.

"I was counting on you for help, and I get none — none from you either!" her eyes seemed to say. She wasn't surprised that he had come; she didn't fully register his arrival. His being there had nothing to do with her suffering or with easing it. The contractions started again and Mary Bogdanovna advised Prince Andrew to leave the room.
The doctor arrived. Prince Andrew went out and, meeting Princess Mary, joined her again. They began talking in whispers, but their conversation kept breaking off. They waited and listened.
"Go to her, dear," said Princess Mary.

Prince Andrew went back to his wife and sat waiting in the room next to hers. A woman came out of the bedroom with a frightened face and became flustered when she saw Prince Andrew. He covered his face with his hands and stayed like that for several minutes. Pitiful, helpless, animal moans came through the door. Prince Andrew stood up, went to the door, and tried to open it. Someone was holding it shut from inside.
"You can't come in! You can't!" said a terrified voice from within.

He began pacing the room. The screaming stopped, and a few more seconds passed. Then suddenly a terrible shriek — it couldn't be hers, she couldn't scream like that — came from the bedroom. Prince Andrew ran to the door; the scream cut off and he heard the wail of a newborn.
"Why have they brought a baby in there?" thought Prince Andrew in the first instant. "A baby? What baby...? Why is there a baby? Or has the baby been born?"

Then suddenly he grasped the joyful meaning of that cry. Tears choked him, and leaning his elbows on the windowsill, he began to weep, sobbing like a child. The door opened. The doctor emerged with his sleeves rolled up, without his coat, pale and with a trembling jaw. Prince Andrew turned to him, but the doctor gave him a dazed look and walked past without a word. A woman rushed out and, seeing Prince Andrew, hesitated on the threshold. He went into his wife's room. She was lying dead, in the same position he had seen her in five minutes before. Despite the fixed stare and the pallor of her cheeks, the same expression remained on her lovely, childlike face with its upper lip covered in fine dark hair.
"I love everyone, and I've never harmed anyone — and what have you done to me?" said her beautiful, pitiful, lifeless face.
In a corner of the room something red and tiny grunted and squealed in Mary Bogdanovna's trembling white hands.

Two hours later Prince Andrew, stepping softly, went into his father's room. The old man already knew everything. He was standing near the door, and as soon as it opened, his rough old arms closed like a vise around his son's neck. Without a word, he began to sob like a child.

Three days later the little princess was buried, and Prince Andrew went up the steps to where the coffin stood to give her a final kiss. There in the coffin lay the same face, though now with closed eyes. "Ah, what have you done to me?" it still seemed to say. And Prince Andrew felt something give way in his soul — he was guilty of a sin he could neither undo nor forget. He couldn't weep. The old man came up too and kissed the small waxen hands lying quietly crossed on her chest, and to him as well her face seemed to say: "Ah, what have you done to me, and why?" And at the sight, the old man turned angrily away.

Another five days passed, and then the young Prince Nicholas Andreevich was baptized. The wet nurse held the coverlet with her chin while the priest used a goose feather to anoint the baby's small red, wrinkled soles and palms.

His grandfather, who was his godfather, trembling and afraid of dropping him, carried the infant around the battered tin font and handed him over to the godmother, Princess Mary. Prince Andrew sat in another room, faint with fear that the baby might be dropped into the font, and waited for the ceremony to end. He looked up joyfully at the baby when the nurse brought him over, and nodded his approval when she told him that the wax with the baby's hair had not sunk in the font but had floated.

title: Book Four (1806) — Chapter 11
paragraphs: On the third day after Christmas, Nicholas dined at home — something he'd rarely done lately. It was a grand farewell dinner, since he and Denisov were leaving to rejoin their regiment after Epiphany. About twenty people were present, including Dolokhov and Denisov.

Never had love so filled the air, and never had the romantic atmosphere been felt so strongly in the Rostov house as during this holiday season. "Seize the moments of happiness — love and be loved! That is the only reality in the world; all else is foolishness. It is the one thing we care about here," said the spirit of the place.

Nicholas, having worn out two pairs of horses as usual without managing to visit all the places he'd meant to go and had been invited to, returned home just before dinner. The moment he walked in, he noticed and felt the charged romantic atmosphere in the house, and also a peculiar awkwardness among some of those present. Sonya, Dolokhov, and the old countess were especially unsettled, and to a lesser degree Natasha. Nicholas understood that something must have happened between Sonya and Dolokhov before dinner, and with the instinctive kindness natural to him, he was very gentle and careful with both of them throughout the meal. That same evening, there was to be one of the holiday balls given by Iogel, the dancing master, for his students.
"Nicholas, will you come to Iogel's? Please do!" said Natasha. "He invited you, and Vasili Dmitrich* is coming too."
* Denisov.
"Where would I not go at the countess's command!" said Denisov, who had playfully taken on the role of Natasha's knight at the Rostovs'. "I'm even weady to dance the pas de châle."
"If I have time," Nicholas answered. "But I promised the Arkharovs — they're having a party."
"And you?" he asked Dolokhov, but as soon as the question was out, he realized he shouldn't have asked it.
"Perhaps," Dolokhov replied coldly and angrily, glancing at Sonya. Then, with a scowl, he gave Nicholas the same kind of look he had given Pierre at the club dinner.
"Something's going on," thought Nicholas, and this impression was confirmed when Dolokhov left immediately after dinner. He found Natasha and asked her what was the matter.
"I was actually looking for you," said Natasha, running out to him. "I told you, but you wouldn't believe me," she said triumphantly. "He proposed to Sonya!"

Though Nicholas hadn't paid much attention to Sonya lately, something seemed to break inside him at this news. Dolokhov was a suitable and in some ways a brilliant match for a girl who was penniless and an orphan. From the perspective of the old countess and society in general, it was unthinkable for her to refuse him. And so Nicholas's first reaction on hearing the news was anger at Sonya. He tried to say, "That's wonderful — of course she'll forget her childhood promises and accept the offer." But before he could get the words out, Natasha continued.
"And imagine — she refused him! Flat out!" she added after a pause. "She told him she loved someone else."
"Yes, my Sonya could never have done anything else!" thought Nicholas.
"No matter how much Mama pushed her, she refused. And I know she won't change her mind once she's decided..."
"And Mama pushed her!" said Nicholas reproachfully.
"Yes," said Natasha. "Do you know, Nicholas — don't be angry — but I know you won't marry her. I know it, heaven knows how, but I'm absolutely certain you won't marry her."
"You don't know anything of the sort!" said Nicholas. "But I need to talk to her. What a darling Sonya is!" he added with a smile.
"Oh, she really is a darling! I'll send her to you."
And Natasha kissed her brother and ran off.

A minute later Sonya came in looking frightened, guilty, and anxious. Nicholas went up to her and kissed her hand. This was the first time since his return that they had spoken alone about their love.

"Sophie," he began, timidly at first and then with growing confidence, "if you want to refuse someone who is not only a brilliant and advantageous match but a wonderful, noble man... he is my friend..."
Sonya interrupted him.
"I've already refused," she said quickly.
"If you're refusing because of me, I'm afraid that I..."
Sonya interrupted him again. She gave him an imploring, frightened look.
"Nicholas, don't say that!" she said.

"No, but I have to. It may seem arrogant, but it's better to be honest. If you're refusing him on my account, I have to tell you the whole truth. I love you, and I think I love you more than anyone else..."
"That is enough for me," said Sonya, blushing.

"No, but I've been in love a thousand times and will fall in love again, though I've never felt the same friendship, trust, and love for anyone as I feel for you. And I'm young. Mama doesn't approve. In short, I make no promise. And I ask you to consider Dolokhov's offer," he said, struggling to pronounce his friend's name.
"Don't say that to me! I want nothing. I love you as a brother and always will, and I want nothing more."
"You're an angel — I'm not worthy of you, but I'm afraid of misleading you."
And Nicholas kissed her hand again.

title: Book Four (1806) — Chapter 12
paragraphs: Iogel's balls were the most enjoyable in Moscow. The mothers said so as they watched their children performing the steps they'd just learned. The boys and girls themselves said so as they danced until they could barely stand. And the older young men and women who came with an air of superiority also agreed — these were the best balls around. That year, two marriages had resulted from these dances. The two pretty young Princesses Gortchakov had met their future husbands there, which only added to the reputation of these events. What set them apart from other balls was the absence of a host or hostess, replaced by the good-natured Iogel himself, fluttering about like a feather, bowing with perfect form as he collected tickets from his guests. Only people who genuinely wanted to dance came — people who still felt the pure delight that thirteen- and fourteen-year-old girls feel when wearing long dresses for the first time. With few exceptions, all the girls were — or seemed to be — pretty, their smiles so radiant and their eyes so bright. Sometimes the best students, led by the exceptionally graceful Natasha, even danced the pas de châle, but at this particular ball only the écossaise, the anglaise, and the mazurka — which was just coming into fashion — were performed. Iogel had rented a ballroom in Bezukhov's house, and everyone agreed the ball was a great success. There were many pretty girls, and the Rostov girls were among the prettiest. Both were especially happy and glowing that evening. Sonya, proud of Dolokhov's proposal, her refusal, and her conversation with Nicholas, had twirled about at home so much that the maid could barely braid her hair. She was radiant with impulsive joy.
Natasha, no less proud of wearing her first long dress and of attending a real ball, was even happier. They were both dressed in white muslin with pink ribbons.

Natasha fell in love the very moment she entered the ballroom. She wasn't in love with anyone in particular — she was in love with everyone. Whatever person she happened to look at, she was in love with them for that instant.
"Oh, how wonderful this is!" she kept saying, running up to Sonya.
Nicholas and Denisov were walking back and forth, watching the dancers with kindly approval.
"How sweet she is — she'll be a weal beauty!" said Denisov.
"Who?"
"Countess Natasha," Denisov answered.
"And how she dances! Such gwace!" he said again after a pause.
"Who are you talking about?"
"Your sister," Denisov said irritably.
Rostov smiled.

"My dear count, you were one of my best students — you must dance," said little Iogel, coming up to Nicholas. "Look at all these charming young ladies —" He made the same request to Denisov, who had also been his student.
"No, my dear fellow, I'll be a wallflower," said Denisov. "Don't you wecollect how badly I used your lessons?"
"Oh no!" said Iogel, rushing to reassure him. "You were only inattentive, but you had talent — oh yes, real talent!"

The band struck up the newly fashionable mazurka. Nicholas couldn't refuse Iogel and asked Sonya to dance. Denisov settled in with the older ladies and, leaning on his saber and tapping time with his foot, entertained them with funny stories while watching the young people dance. Iogel and Natasha — his pride and best student — were the first couple on the floor. Moving noiselessly on his little feet in low shoes, Iogel glided across the hall with Natasha, who, though shy, performed her steps with care. Denisov didn't take his eyes off her, beating time with his saber in a way that made clear: if he wasn't dancing, it was because he chose not to, not because he couldn't. In the middle of a figure, he beckoned to Rostov as he passed by:
"This is not how it's done," he said. "What sort of Polish mazuwka is this? But she does dance splendidly."
Knowing that Denisov had a reputation — even in Poland — for his masterful mazurka, Nicholas ran up to Natasha:
"Go choose Denisov. He's a real dancer — a marvel!" he said.

When Natasha's turn came to choose a partner, she stood up and, running quickly across the floor in her little bow-trimmed shoes, hurried shyly to the corner where Denisov sat. She saw that everyone was watching her, waiting. Nicholas could see Denisov refusing, though he was smiling with delight. He ran over to them.
"Please, Vasili Dmitrich," Natasha was saying, "please come!"
"Oh no, let me off, Countess," Denisov replied.
"Come on, Vaska," said Nicholas.
"They're coaxing me like I'm Vaska the cat!" Denisov said jokingly.
"I'll sing for you the whole evening," said Natasha.

"Oh, the faiwy! She can do anything with me!" said Denisov, and he unhooked his saber. He emerged from behind the chairs, clasped his partner's hand firmly, threw back his head, and positioned his foot, waiting for the beat. Only on horseback and in the mazurka was Denisov's short stature invisible — he looked like the dashing figure he felt himself to be. At the right beat, he glanced sideways at his partner with a merry, triumphant look, suddenly stamped one foot, bounced from the floor like a ball, and flew around the room with his partner. He glided silently on one foot across half the floor, and seeming not to notice the chairs, appeared about to crash straight into them when suddenly — clinking his spurs and spreading his legs wide — he stopped dead on his heels, stood still for a second, stamped in place with a clank of spurs, whirled rapidly around, and striking his left heel against his right, flew off in a circle again. Natasha guessed what he intended and, giving herself over to his lead, followed instinctively, hardly knowing how. He spun her first one way then another, holding her with his left hand, then his right. He dropped to one knee and whirled her around him, then leaped up and dashed forward so impetuously it seemed he would fly through every room in the house without taking a breath — and then he suddenly stopped and performed an entirely new and unexpected sequence of steps. When at last he smartly twirled his partner in front of her chair and drew up with a click of his spurs and a bow, Natasha didn't even curtsy in return. She stared at him in amazement, smiling as if she didn't recognize him.
"What was that?" she managed to say.

Although Iogel wouldn't officially acknowledge it as a proper mazurka, everyone was thrilled by Denisov's skill. He was asked again and again to dance, and the older guests began reminiscing with smiles about Poland and the good old days. Denisov, flushed from the mazurka and mopping himself with his handkerchief, sat down beside Natasha and didn't leave her side for the rest of the evening.
